speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It is an important part of Singapore’s criminal law.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The nature and complexity of crime have also changed, and it is timely that we update the Penal Code to ensure continued relevance and effectiveness.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Penal Code Review Committee (PCRC) comprised lawyers, academics, judges and Ministry officials.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We considered the proposals by the PCRC and sought feedback from a wide range of stakeholders and also the general public.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: More than 700 stakeholders from the social, religious, financial, legal and education sectors were engaged in various dialogue sessions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We received written feedback from various individuals and organisations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We have also made the Bill available to Members of this House and to the public for the last three months.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We are heartened by the general support for the proposals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: My speech today will cover four key areas: updating current sexual offences; updating the Penal Code's definitions and removing outmoded offences; dealing with emerging crime trends; and updating the sentencing framework.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Minister Shanmugam will cover the Government's views on two key areas: enhancement of protection for vulnerable victims and reviewing sexual offences, specifically, offences against minors and new sexual offences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: On updating current sexual offences, first, let me talk about the offence of rape.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, the offence of rape covers only penile penetration of the vagina.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We take the view that the label of "rape" is appropriate for non-consensual acts involving penile penetration of the anus and mouth.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This reflects the high degree of violation and the physical and health risks involved.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: With this Bill, both men and women can be victims of rape.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, the Bill further clarifies the law on "consent" in the context of sexual offences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 121 sets out three misconceptions of fact that would vitiate consent: sexual nature of the act; sexual purpose of the act; and identity of the perpetrator doing the act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We decided not to have a positive statutory definition of consent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Section 90 of the Penal Code currently sets out the situations where consent is negated.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There is a good body of case law on this matter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Turning to the second key area in the Penal Code review, the updating of the Code to reflect shifting societal values.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, marital immunity for rape is only removed in certain circumstances, where there has been a breakdown in the marriage.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Sexual relations in a marriage and, indeed, in any relationship, should be based on mutual consent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Sexual assault is violence, and violence in any context is wrong.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is the basis on which we have repealed marital immunity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 110 and 112 of the Bill deal with this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There have been concerns raised that the complete repeal of marital immunity for rape could lead to an abuse of the legal process, due to an increase in unmeritorious allegations of rape by vindictive spouses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I want to assure the House that all allegations of rape will be held to the same high standard of evidential rigour.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There is a separate proposal which goes some way to deal with this concern.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We have doubled the maximum punishment for section 182 of the Penal Code – situations where persons give false information to a public servant – from one to two years' imprisonment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In other words, persons who knowingly make false reports will be dealt with firmly by the law.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This proposal received wide public support, including from organisations which work directly with persons who attempt suicides, such as the Samaritans of Singapore (SOS).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The criminal justice system is not the best way to deal with persons who are so distressed that they choose to end their own lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In fact, the threat of prosecution, and the labelling of persons who attempt suicide as "offenders" may worsen their emotional state and the stigma they face.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This view was shared by PCRC and many others during the public consultation process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There were some concerns that the decriminalisation of attempted suicide would reduce the deterrent effect and cause an increased number of suicides.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, bear in mind that persons who attempt suicide typically are so distressed that the deterrent effect of criminalisation is very low.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The present situation is that hardly anyone is prosecuted and punished for this offence in the first place.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There were also concerns that the decriminalisation of attempted suicide will send a signal that the Government has shifted its position on the sanctity of life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I assure you that this is not the case.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Every effort will still be made to prevent suicides.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill amends other laws to ensure that the Police will still be able to intervene in suicide situations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Members of the public will still be able to call for emergency assistance in cases where a person is attempting suicide.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The offence of abetment of attempted suicide will be retained.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under this Bill, the maximum imprisonment term for abetment of attempted suicide will be enhanced significantly from one year to 10 years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Where the abetment of attempted suicide is of a minor or a person who lacks mental capacity, higher maximum punishments will apply – 15 years' imprisonment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 84, 85, 89, 180 and 183 give effect to this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill codifies the definitions of fault elements, such as intention, knowledge and dishonesty.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These definitions crystallise and clarify the existing case law.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We wanted to make the law clearer since most of these definitions apply to offences outside the Penal Code as well.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The amendments in clauses 21 and 22 will not change the existing law.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There are two types of mistake – mistake of fact and mistake of law.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, it will continue to be the case that ignorance of law and mistake of law will not be a defence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, to be clear, we have clarified expressly, in clauses 110 and 111, the current position at law on the defence of mistake as to consent for the offences of rape and sexual assault by penetration.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Where the accused person proves that he made a mistake in good faith such that he believed that the act of penetration was done with consent, he will not be liable for the offence of rape or sexual assault by penetration.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In other words, the amendments in clauses 110 and 111 will make clear the burden of proof remains on the accused person to prove on the balance of probabilities that he was mistaken in good faith that there was consent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The amendments will not affect other presumptions which exist in law today, such as those in the Misuse of Drugs Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We will address an anomaly in the defence of intoxication in section 86.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This was pointed out by the High Court in Juma'at bin Samad v PP.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: With the amendment, intoxication must be taken into account in determining the accused person's "knowledge" or "belief", in addition to "intention".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I wish to make clear that all other aspects of the law on intoxication in Juma'at are preserved.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Explanatory Statement is not clear in this regard, and this speech clarifies the intent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The current MACR is seven years old, and this is a colonial inheritance, since 1872.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We need to strike a balance between protection of the public and fairness to young children who may not be able to understand the consequences of their action.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There is no international consensus on the appropriate MACR.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The MACR of seven years old is on the lower end of the spectrum.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In Singapore, criminal activity among children below the age of 10 is very low.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We see increased criminal activity from the age of 10 onwards, and most juveniles commit property offences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: On balance, we think an MACR of 10 years old would be more appropriate in our context.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Children below 10, and those between 10 and 12 who are not mature enough to understand the nature and consequences of their conduct, will not be convicted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: But this does not mean that we do nothing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We are looking to develop a framework to allow us to intervene in cases of such young children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The raising of MACR will take effect when the framework for rehabilitation of these young children has been finalised.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 25 and 26 give effect to this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I will now move on to the third key area on how the Penal Code will be amended to deal with emerging crime trends, especially in the area of white-collar offences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Offences can be committed across national borders, with the constituent elements of offences committed in different countries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Indeed, many white-collar offences have multiple physical elements which can take place in different countries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It is currently not clear whether Singapore Courts will have jurisdiction when some elements take place in Singapore, and others outside of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A new Schedule will be inserted into the Penal Code.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 2 and 168 give effect to this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill introduces the new offence of fraud.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To understand the need for fraud offences, we need to look at the current offence of cheating.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The offence relies on there being a victim that relied on the deception by the offender.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The deception had to induce the victim to do something.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Take, for instance, the London inter-bank lending rate (LIBOR)-fixing scandal in the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It would be very difficult to show that the victims relied upon the fraudulent representations of the bank employees who manipulated LIBOR.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Calculations for LIBOR are complicated and may not be understood by these victims.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Yet, the LIBOR-fixing scandal is egregious, with far-reaching consequences on financial markets and products.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We must be able to take action against such dishonest behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The new offence of fraud is intended to deal with novel and complex schemes which the current offence of cheating may not cover.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It focuses on the deceitful intent of the offender and not the effect on the alleged victim.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The cheating offence will continue to be used where the elements of the offence are satisfied.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The second category of other types of fraud will come into force first, with the rest of the Penal Code amendments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For fraud in connection with contracts for goods and services, we are working on the development of a mechanism, which allows private persons to obtain recourse for more common cases involving smaller losses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This mechanism may involve private prosecutions, civil claims or some other avenues.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The new fraud offence has been adapted from the UK's Fraud Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 138 and 139 give effect to this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The experience of the UK in the implementation of the fraud offence has been positive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It has enabled the UK government to respond to technologically-enabled and complex forms of fraud.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: While these would fall within the definition of fraud, most of these offences are committed by perpetrators overseas.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For such cases, prevention is better than cure.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: While the Police will continue to clamp down on scam activities and work actively with our foreign counterparts, it is a fact that it is challenging to bring these foreign perpetrators to task.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We have made some amendments to the sentencing framework to ensure that the sentences prescribed are proportionate to the seriousness of the offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Members of this House will be familiar with mandatory minimum sentences (MMS).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: MMS refers to a sentence where the law mandates that a judge must impose a minimum jail term or another sentence, such as caning, for a particular offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It enhances deterrence for serious offences by imposing certain, predictable sentences on offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We recognise that society has become safer, less violent and more mature.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: MMS will also be retained for offences which attract a mandatory sentence of caning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These offences are serious and generally involve elements of physical confrontation and violence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Only first-time offenders will qualify for presumptive minimum sentences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For these offenders, the Court may sentence them to a punishment which is less than MMS in exceptional circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We have provided guidance in the law on exceptional circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Where the accused person is a first-time offender, pleaded guilty and where he was of previous good character – the mere presence of all or any of these factors will not be sufficient to constitute exceptional circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Court will determine what exceptional circumstances are.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, Courts can already exercise judicial mercy in very rare cases where humanitarian considerations arise.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This gives us an idea of the degree of exceptionality that is required.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The introduction of presumptive minimum sentences is not a softening of the Government's stance against such crimes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Because exceptional circumstances must be shown, we anticipate that the majority of offenders who commit these offences will still face the prescribed minimum sentence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In this major review of the Penal Code, we have clarified existing concepts and amended our laws to reflect prevailing norms and better respond to our changing environment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Minister Shanmugam will provide the Government's views on the changes to two key areas: sexual offences and enhancing protection of the most vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary has given the Government's view on some of the key proposed amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I intend to set out the Government’s position on two major areas of the law which we are amending.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One, better protection of vulnerable victims; and second, dealing with sexual offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are setting out new offences and enhancing penalties where minors are involved.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some additional conduct of a sexual nature will be specifically criminalised.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We want to provide stronger protection for those who cannot protect themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, we will enhance maximum punishment for offences committed against such victims.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, we will introduce new offences where such victims are abused.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members of this House will remember the case of Annie Ee.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They made her do all the household chores and they kept her salary.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She suffered for eight months and then she died.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: With the new amendments, if a person like Annie Ee is assessed to be substantially unable to protect herself, then her abusers will be liable to up to twice the maximum punishment.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They will be charged for the offence of voluntarily causing grievous hurt; so up to 20 years' imprisonment.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is in clause 17 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That will allow the Police to intervene quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Penalties will also be enhanced for specific offences committed against persons who are in an intimate or close relationship with the offender, even if they are not married.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Promoting Alternatives to Violence (PAVE) is a voluntary welfare organisation (VWO) which works closely with a variety of other agencies, including the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They told me about this case, which was one of the reasons why I decided we ought to change the law here.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They helped a lady by the name of Cindy.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Cindy had suffered horrific abuse from her live-in partner.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She was found by the Police in the year 2000, almost completely blind, with slash wounds all over her body and with broken bones.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She had suffered horrific abuse over the eight years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The two young children she had with the abuser witnessed all of this abuse, which took place almost daily.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In many serious domestic abuse cases, the abuser exploits the trust of the victim to abuse them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The victims often find it difficult to leave such partners due to the emotional and psychological manipulation which is frequently found in such relationships.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These amendments will mean that such perpetrators who abuse victims, where the victims trust and depend on them, the abusers will face much more severe punishments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These amendments must be read or looked at together with the proposed amendments to the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA), which will be coming up for Second Reading tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It means that such intimate partners can get Personal Protection Orders (PPOs) on an expedited basis and that perpetrators will get more severe penalties.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Previously, only married partners can apply for PPOs under the Women's Charter.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Now, under the proposed amendments to POHA, the timelines for getting a PPO will be comparable to that under the Women's Charter.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, intimate partners, usually women, who are in a relationship but not married, who fear violence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is a significant step towards giving them greater protection.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Again, based on Parliamentary rules, I cannot go too much into the details on POHA.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But my intention is that it must be fast, it must be quick, and they must be able to get remedies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My colleague, Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong, will take Parliament through POHA tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the Penal Code, new offences in respect of abuse of vulnerable victims which lead to death or other forms of grievous hurt will also be introduced.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But going back to intimate partners, therefore, on the one side, the penalties to be enhanced; and on the other side, easier access to PPOs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Of course, there is the underlying psychological problem, that if the woman does not want to leave and continues to suffer the abuse, then our agencies or the VWOs will have to try to find a way of identifying this woman – usually women – and then, encourage them to take the steps.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Now, I am moving on to the abuse leading to death of vulnerable victims.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: New offences are being introduced, where there is serious abuse of vulnerable victims.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I remind Members of another case, Daniel Nasser, two years old.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was abused by his mother and her live-in boyfriend over a period of at least five weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They kicked and slapped him almost every day.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The autopsy found 31 external injuries on Daniel.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court said the couple had inflicted harm "in a ruthless and unrelenting manner".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In such serious cases of abuse which leads to the death of the vulnerable victim, Members will find it odd, but lawyers will know, it is not easy to convict the offenders of murder.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The reason is that it is difficult to show that they had the requisite mens rea, that is, the mental elements that were present to meet the requirements for the conviction for murder.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think we have to take a strong stance against such abuse.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I refer to clauses 83, 104 and 171.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Persons who have custody, care or charge of the victims.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have a responsibility to protect those under their care from harm.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Victims, as I described earlier, are children, domestic workers and other vulnerable persons.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The offence deals with situations where two or more persons were in a position to cause the death of the victim but both deny they were the ones who caused the ill-treatment.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In such cases, it is very difficult to prove in Court who committed the abuse and who permitted the abuse.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Currently, when there is this sort of ambiguity, both could get acquitted, while there is a dead child.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Deaths resulting from natural causes or accidents will not be covered.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, otherwise, if you stood by and you allowed a child to be abused in this way, you can be charged.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The United Kingdom (UK) and Australia have similar offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A case from the UK is illustrative of the kind of situation we are thinking about.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was living with his father and his father’s female partner.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The boy suffered 21 different injuries within 48 hours before his death, including a fatal fracture to the left femur.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It occurred within 12 hours prior to his death.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was established that only the father and his partner were present during the period when the fatal injury was inflicted.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The father had been absent for around two hours.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Both defendants were charged for murder, and both claimed they did not to know how the injuries were sustained.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Singapore, under our proposed amendments, the father and partner both can be charged for causing or allowing a young child's death.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, Members can look at clauses 83, 104 and 171.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There have been some feedback and concerns that persons who are themselves victims of abuse could, nevertheless, be held liable for their inaction by "failing to protect" a vulnerable victim or "causing or allowing the death of a vulnerable victim".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, a husband violently abuses his wife and his children.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The concern is that the abused wife may herself be found liable under this offence if she did not intervene to prevent her husband from abusing the children.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is even though she may not have really been in a position to intervene.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court needs to determine the steps the accused person could have been reasonably expected to have taken to prevent the abuse of the vulnerable victim.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Under the amendments, Daniel Nasser's abusers, the very people who were supposed to protect him, could be liable for the new offence of causing death by sustained abuse, and causing or allowing Daniel’s death.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Now, I will turn to the area of sexual offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are amendments to better protect minors and there are amendments creating new categories of sexual offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members of this House may remember the case of Joshua Robinson.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was 39 years old, he met two 15-year-old girls on social networking sites.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He pressured them to send him nude pictures of themselves and to meet up to have sex with him.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When his house was raided, they found obscene films, including more than 300 films of child pornography.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After he was arrested and released on bail, when he was on bail, Joshua Robinson showed a six-year-old girl explicit videos of his girlfriend performing a sexual act on him.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At present, that is not a separate category of offence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will have to come within the rubric of showing an obscene film.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I think Members will agree that we should criminalise it separately and clearly, rather than treating it as just showing an obscene film.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think the action and acts are heinous in themselves, beyond the showing of the film.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Joshua Robinson was eventually sentenced to imprisonment for having sex with minors because both girls were under 16, making and possessing obscene films, and showing an obscene film to a six-year-old girl.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think Members will agree that getting the two 15-year-old girls to send nude photos should itself be criminalised, and showing an obscene film to a six-year-old should be treated with more severity by a separate category of offence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, I said at that time that we needed to look at criminalising some parts of his conduct, which were not caught at that time, and increasing the penalties as well, to ensure that people like Joshua Robinson will be dealt with more severely through higher penalties.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the new offences, under the rubric of "exploitative sexual activity with minors" will deal with sexual predators who exploit young people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The age of consent for sexual activity is 16 years old, but there are situations where slightly older minors, those between 16 and 18 years old, may be exploited for sexual gratification by persons who are in relationships of trust with the minor.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are two parts to this definition of "exploitation".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, in considering whether the accused is in a relationship that is exploitative of the victim, the Court will be required to consider the age of the minor.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The younger the person, that is the victim, the more susceptible to influence he or she will be.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, the difference in age between the accused and the minor.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A large age difference may result in the victim viewing the accused as an authority figure, allowing the accused to exert significant influence over the victim.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the accused initiates sexual communication or activity, it is likely that the intention of the accused, particularly if it is done very early in the relationship, was to make use of the power imbalance in the relationship to exploit the victim for his sexual gratification.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Fourth, the degree of control or influence exercised by the accused over the minor.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The greater the influence by the accused over the minor, the more the minor's will may be considered to be compromised.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The use of violence or coercion by the accused will be considered to be amongst the indicators of control or domination over the victim.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, in short, a key factor in determining "exploitation" is the presence of a power imbalance between the accused person and the minor.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are other jurisdictions which take a different approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, the UK and some states in Australia have an exhaustive list of relationships; sexual activity between adults and minors in such relationships is prohibited.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have adapted this as the second part of the definition of "exploitation".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A list of specified relationships has been included in the law.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Where these relationships exist between the accused and the minor, there will be a rebuttable presumption that an exploitative relationship exists.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They involve an adult who is in a position of responsibility, authority or influence over the minor.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Where the relationship between the accused person and the minor is not in this list, the Court can still find that a relationship was exploitative based on its assessment by reference to the first part of the definition.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if you look at clauses 113 and 121, those are set out.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will now turn to predatory conduct against minors.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The amendments and new offences take into account developments in technology which have enabled predators to increase their number of victims and the speed at which they can groom minors.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: New offences will be introduced: sexual communication with minors – I spoke about this earlier – and showing a minor a sexual image.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Also, sexual activity in the presence of a minor – clause 117.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, this will allow us to criminalise predatory behaviour like Joshua Robinson's, including asking minors to send him nude images.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There will be, of course, other types of conduct, like sexual experimentation amongst young persons.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not the intent of these new offences to target these groups of persons.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) will, of course, have to exercise prosecutorial discretion in determining whether it is in the public interest to prosecute.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When it is between boyfriend and girlfriend, and they are of a certain age, very young, and it is not exploitative, it should not come within these provisions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Covering the spectrum of predatory behaviour allows us to intervene early to ensure that our children are protected before the offender has time to meet them and prepare them, and commit additional, more serious sexual offences that could cause, of course, greater physical and psychological harm.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I said in this House last year that we were looking into drafting specific laws against child abuse material.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Apart from sexual abuse, some children are physically abused; they are tortured as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Terrible harm is caused to these children who are used in the production of such material.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We must do what we can to protect them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This does not happen much in Singapore, but we are going to make this extraterritorial in some ways.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have criminalised the spectrum of offences to deal with every person involved, from consumers to the producers of such material.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we will also cover realistic depictions of children, meaning depictions which so closely resemble that of actual children, such that if an ordinary person looks at the depiction, they cannot tell whether this is real or a depiction.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Inclusion of these realistic depictions of children will prevent an accused person from arguing that a depiction is computer-generated when, in fact, it involved an actual child.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The offences will cover Singaporeans and Permanent Residents who commit such offences overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Of course, it will cover them if they do it here as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Any person who is in Singapore and commits these offences against a child overseas, and any person who is overseas and commits these offences against a child in Singapore, those are in clause 120.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Next, child abuse material which depicts fictional children.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is dealt with under section 292 of the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The offence criminalises sale, distribution, exhibition, production of obscene material.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Possession of such material is not criminalised under this provision.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We want to enhance punishments under section 292 when the obscene object depicts minors below 16 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These refer to anatomically accurate dolls or robots with features which resemble a minor below 16 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are prohibiting them because of the concern that they may reinforce tendencies which can then develop into actual harmful acts towards children.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Next, technology has facilitated the commission of sexual offences, such as voyeurism, "cyber-flashing", distribution of intimate images often referred to as "revenge pornography".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And there has been an increase in such cases.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These offences are currently criminalised under the Films Act and the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We want to create specific offences in the Penal Code to provide proper framing for such offences and adequate punishments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Voyeurism involves observation or recording of someone doing a private act without the person's consent.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some of the more commonly known forms of voyeurism include "up-skirting" and "down-blousing".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Recently, there has been spotlight on these offences because of the incident in the National University of Singapore involving Nicholas Lim.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These offences are currently dealt with under "Insult of Modesty" in the Penal Code and the Films Act.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The current laws, in my view, do not adequately address the range of offences involving voyeuristic recordings and the distribution of such material on the Internet.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we propose to introduce specific offences involving "voyeurism" which will define the offending behaviour and provide for adequate punishments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The proposals, Members know, as I said earlier this afternoon, well pre-date the incident involving Nicholas Lim.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In fact, the Bill was tabled in Parliament before that incident became public.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was before the incident took place as well, in terms of working on it and drafting.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Where the accused person has made a recording of another person doing a private act, or of their private parts, it will be presumed that the person being recorded or observed did not consent to the observation or recording.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Sometimes, there are evidential challenges because you can find the images, but you cannot identify who the person is.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This will get over the legal burden, and the presumption will be that there was no consent.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The accused can then say why there was consent.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The new offences will criminalise "Peeping Tom" behaviour, making of voyeuristic recordings, distribution, possession of, or gaining access to such recordings.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Also, modifying any part of a building's structure to make voyeuristic recordings will also be criminalised specifically.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This was recently reported in the international media as being a very serious issue in South Korea.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is double the current maximum one-year punishment for the offence of insulting modesty under section 509.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is, I think, a clear need to deter the proliferation of voyeuristic recordings.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, distribution of voyeuristic recordings will attract a higher punishment – a maximum imprisonment term of five years if you go around distributing these.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court may also impose a fine and caning for these offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have also introduced a new offence to criminalise sexual exposure which is commonly known as "flashing".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There has been prevalence of this – persons intentionally sending unsolicited pictures of their genitalia over social media or via messaging platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Penalties for this offence will be enhanced where the victim is below 14 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Distribution or threat to distribute intimate images – we will introduce a new offence for distribution, threat to distribute, colloquially known as "revenge porn".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Intimate images could become widely shared on platforms, and it may be impossible to completely remove them, and they have the potential to cause great harm to the victim.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The offence will exclude images, such as caricatures or cartoons of a person performing a sexual act.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, a lewd caricature of a person may amount to harassment, but not something that could be mistaken as an "intimate image" of the person depicted.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Where the offence is committed against a person below 14 years old, imprisonment will be made mandatory.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The new offence will also cover cases where a person unlawfully accesses databases or recordings that contain intimate images.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are also introducing a new offence: procurement of sexual activity by deception relating to two types of conduct.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, the use of sexually protective measures; and second, the presence or absence of sexually transmitted diseases.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The amendments we are making today strengthen our laws.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They will help ensure that Singapore continues to be a safe home for our people, particularly women, children and vulnerable persons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is the result of an immense effort by the many stakeholders – the Ministry of Law (MinLaw), Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), AGC, the Law Society, the Criminal Bar and members of the public who have provided the valuable feedback.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The product is a formidable piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first theme is the protection of victims in vulnerable positions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, vulnerable victims who are unable to defend themselves, victims of abuse within a marriage and minors who have been victimised by abusive or lewd acts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some of us remember the case of Annie Ee.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Annie was a 26-year-old waitress with intellectual disabilities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: She was physically and psychologically abused by her flatmates for eight months until she died with severe injuries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This law will ensure the perpetrators in a case like Annie Ee's will be dealt with accurately and effectively, matching culpability with an appropriate sentence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Robinson had even shown a six-year-old girl an obscene video while her father was training at a gym.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That clause introduces the offence of sexual activity or image in the presence of a minor below 16 years of age.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is relevant to the proposed section 376ED and it should be supported.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During the debate on the Penal Code (Amendment) Bill in 2007, Ms Ellen Lee raised the point that the exceptions to marital rape immunity are inadequate to address serious abuse in marriage.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, Ms Ellen Lee cited the case of PP against N where the marital relationship was already highly strained and the husband forcefully dragged her back to their matrimonial home, tied her hands, gagged her and "raped" her.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The changes to section 375(4) in clause 110(b) address that and put into clear focus the victim’s interest.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a bold move and should be supported.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am also glad that Ms Ellen Lee’s conscientious voice in 2007 has made an impact on the changes we are discussing today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many countries talk about the rights of the accused.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yes, that is important, but a good justice system is also victim-focused.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore-hosted webpages saw an exponential increase in child pornography content.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the first 10 months of 2017, this number almost doubled to 412.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The amendments to this Bill improve our law’s capability to deter such lewd content and punish the purveyors of it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are innocent and must be shielded from depraved and corrupt humans who seek offensive pleasure from such lewd acts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, the proposed sections 377BG to 377BK, which punish purveyors of child pornography or child abuse content, are important and timely.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One key way is to tackle crimes committed through the Internet.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The proposed section 4B(1)(c) does so by specifying that certain offences committed outside Singapore but which affect Singapore are punishable as though the act had been carried out in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially useful for financial crimes which can be committed remotely, with no respect for territorial boundaries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This ensures that the arm of Singapore's law can reach overseas actors who create harm in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is key for a highly connected hub, such as Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is an amendment that is needed and welcomed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The new presumptive minimum sentence is another important feature of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At this stage, I should declare that I am a lawyer in private practice and sometimes act as Defence Counsel in criminal cases.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From my experience, it is good to give our judges the discretion to impose accurate sentences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This may involve, at times, lighter sentences where there are strong mitigating factors which put the offenders’ acts in perspective.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allowing a judge to mete out a lower sentence, even lower than the presumptive minimum, could prove very useful where an offender is quite clearly on the lower spectrum of the culpability scale.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, I do have a clarification to ask.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the new subsection 4, it says that "in any written law, unless the context requires otherwise, a reference to a mandatory minimum sentence of imprisonment shall include a reference to a presumptive minimum sentence." Could the Minister elaborate on whether such a rationale applies to all existing regulatory and criminal laws or whether it is restricted to only the laws contained in the Penal Code?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, how would subsection 4 apply to the Misuse of Drugs Act which already has a carefully calibrated deterrent-rehabilitation regime through the availability of the Drug Rehabilitation Centre at one extreme and the Long Term Imprisonments 1 and 2 options at the other extreme?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In short, Sir, presumptive minimum sentences will have the advantage of creating some broad consistency in sentencing across courtrooms and across cases but allows much needed flexibility where the merits of the case justify a lower sentence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While it is good and necessary to carry out an extensive review of our criminal laws every 12 years or so, would MHA and MinLaw consider creating a set of legal tools which could deal with morphing criminal threats of the future?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In a world where technology progresses so rapidly, the potential criminal activities and their modus operandi may be morphing so quickly that even though we have a robust new criminal law framework now, the law may still not be wide enough to address the criminal methodologies of the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, would MHA and MinLaw consider the suggestion to introduce a Schedule or the possibility for subsidiary legislation through which the Minister can respond quickly to the morphing criminal phenomenon without needing to come to Parliament?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, in the Misuse of Drugs Act, the Minister does not need to come to Parliament to update the list of drugs, especially new psychoactive drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this way, the law addressing the harms of drugs is flexible, versatile and able to respond quickly to the threat.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If there was a mechanism for a readily amendable Schedule or subsidiary legislation, and the original offence in the primary legislation was broad enough and consistent with Parliament's intention to encompass such a situation, then rather than having to come to Parliament to amend the provision to plug loopholes, the Minister could expand on the limbs of an existing provision to tighten the law through a Schedule or subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While this cannot apply retrospectively, it would be a quick and efficient way to plug loopholes for future cases.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Could MHA and MinLaw consider this suggestion, please?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since speaking on the topic in Parliament in 2007, I have followed the debate in other countries and studied the multiple legal challenges in various jurisdictions which seek to redefine marriage, gender, adoption rights, spousal rights and what is taught in schools.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has caused me to believe that retaining a provision, such as section 377A, even if it is unenforced, continues to be a good approach for our country.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should build it up and not tear it down.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, my views expressed in 2007 have not changed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yes, attempted suicide is an issue which must be addressed with great sensitivity, and the topic must be respected with all the attendent empathy it so clearly deserves.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, I have looked at the Ministry's arguments for repealing section 309 and I hold a different view.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do I think we should enforce section 309 against people who attempt suicide?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But keeping the provision is still of immense value.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I humbly submit that there are six reasons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, because it sends a normative signal that taking one's life is not the answer to life's problems, to the extent that the law prohibits it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, the repeal of section 309 may send the signal that taking one's life is acceptable to broader society when, in my view, that is not society's thinking.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Three, all the attendant treatment, support, care and counselling can be provided while still retaining the provision.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, when this happens, society would benefit from the deterrent effect of the law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This means that the law would help deter some future suicides in society, while, at the same time, the people who need the counselling and care are able to receive it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I cite the inspiring words of a courageous young lady who wrote a forum page letter in the Straits Times in February 2019.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I quote her: "As someone who overcame suicide and is now a passionate advocate for the sanctity of life, I am sad to see suicide being decriminalised in our nation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Suicide is truly a multifaceted and complex issue, and the law should not be excluded from having a deterrent effect on people who see death as the only option in their difficult circumstances.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I gave up the idea of further suicide attempts after Police officers gently reminded me that attempting suicide was an offence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There was no need for the authorities to restrain or prosecute me, for I was cooperative and clearly in distress.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In recent years, I managed to persuade a young foreigner from killing herself just by informing her the offensive nature of suicide in our nation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Human life is sacred and should not be violated, not even by ourselves." She goes on, "The decriminalisation of suicide perpetuates the erroneous message of 'my body, my choice'.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When it is no longer mandatory to report a suicide attempt, people will stop reporting it as it is not a crime." – Ms Ho Lay Ping.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Writing that and putting a name to it takes immense courage and I respect that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is further value in that story, that real-life story shared by Ms Ho displays why the presence of sections 305 and 306 do not cure the concerns over the decriminalisation of attempted suicide.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourth reason, I agree with the Ministry that the stigma against those suffering from mental health should be removed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, I have spoken up in Parliament about removing such a stigma and increasing community support for those suffering from mental illness in 2018 and 2019.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should not hold mental illness against the person who has it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the removal of section 309 does not need to be part of that destigmatisation exercise.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Broader society will have no legal deterrent and those attempting suicide may consider the absence of a prohibition as a licence to attempt the act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If that were to happen, society loses and we could see an increase in the number of suicides in future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I feel duty-bound to articulate that concern in this House.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This, in my view, should be seriously reconsidered since removing the requirement for the mandatory reporting of an attempted suicide removes one means, a crucial means, by which the suicidal person can get the professional help he or she needs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sixth, the retention of section 309 consolidates the moral position against euthanasia.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For the record, Sir, I support laws that outlaw euthanasia for I believe that an innocent life is as precious through sufferings as it is through joys.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, for all the six reasons above, I ask the Ministry to seriously reconsider whether it wants to repeal section 309.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If the number of suicides in Singapore increases following repeal when compared to pre-repeal numbers, I ask that the Ministry consider re-introducing a provision similar to section 309 back into the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For such a detailed study to be meaningful, mandatory reporting should be re-introduced – it should not be abolished.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In essence, Sir, I urge the Government to closely examine its decision to decriminalise the offence of attempted suicide and closely monitor the impact that it has on our society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My concerns regarding the abolition of section 309 do not dilute, in any way, my strong support for the other excellent facets of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, the other amendments seek to protect vulnerable victims, ensure our muscular law reaches perpetrators who seek to do Singapore harm from beyond our shores, retains section 377A and introduces a sentencing framework which allows for the deployment of more accurate justice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those are strong and commendable initiatives worthy of support.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: The amendments in the Penal Code address various key emerging crime trends and I support these changes.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Under emerging crime trends, I would like to talk about the changes made to tackle voyeurism and the distribution or threat to distribute intimate images.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: In this day and age, with the advancements in technology, filming devices are not just getting more sophisticated but also more readily available.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: It is no longer limited to the conventional bulky devices, or even camera handphones.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, a spy camera could be easily ordered online in many shapes and sizes, such as in the form of a pen, a clock or even a clothing hook.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: These cameras are discrete and would practically go undetected in most circumstances.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Further, our society is increasingly connected to the Internet, making it easy to hide behind a screen to circulate the compromising images captured.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the distribution of these images will reach a wider audience, resulting in greater distress to the victim compared to the past.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Although the current law has some penalties for such behaviour, it was passed at a time where voyeurism was less prevalent, as the technology then did not easily allow it.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: At present times, however, the law does not seem adequate.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Also, as the devices can be more easily concealed, there could be even more cases that go unreported than before.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: As such, there is a need to enhance current penalties in order to deter such behaviour.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I would like to talk about the distribution or threat to distribute intimate images.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: While there has been an effort to educate the public on the dangers of recording images of oneself online in compromising positions, some, especially youths who are more tech-savvy, may land themselves in these situations.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: While filming these images, they were expecting total privacy between the consenting parties.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: However, if things do go sour, these films could be distributed as part of revenge.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: While the victims are able to contact platforms to take the video images down, there could be countless sites hosting these images.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
