text: And it would require time for such action, during which the images could have been seen by a great number of people.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Also, if it falls into the dark web, it could potentially be there forever.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, we need a greater deterrence for this, too, as the distress and hurt caused to the victim would be much greater than in the past.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: To go a step further, the Ministry could consider how to encourage victims of such crimes to come forward and report it to the Police, to prevent the perpetrators from causing more harm.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: We should be mindful not to victim-shame, as this is one of the reasons why such crime goes unreported.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: We should also consider providing support to the victims, such as counselling, where necessary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After the Bill was tabled in Parliament for First Reading in February, the Second Reading was deferred to May, which was useful to give the House more time to study the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party is in general support of the Bill, which makes several broad-based improvements to our primary criminal law, that is, the Penal Code, and to related laws.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To me, there are four aspects particularly worth mentioning.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will give sentencing judges some discretion to depart from the mandatory minimum sentences for offences in certain situations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By introducing some flexibility to the Court, there would be less need for plea bargaining, making justice more transparent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, there are changes to strongly deter and punish crimes against victims who are more vulnerable, such as minors under 14, domestic workers and vulnerable adults.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This has an important signaling effect that society today views marriage as a union between equal partners.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Despite its positives, I have some queries and uncertainty over some aspects of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For today’s debate, I will focus on just two matters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They are: one, the approach towards offences of causing hurt; and two, vulnerable victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the past decades, the offence of voluntarily causing hurt (VCH) under section 323 of the Penal Code has been a non-arrestable offence, meaning that the Police are ordinarily not able to arrest the suspect without a Court warrant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, being a non-arrestable offence, the typical advice given to VCH victims is that the Police will not investigate the matter unless the victim goes to Court to obtain a Magistrate’s order to direct the Police to investigate, or the victim can pursue a private summons against the perpetrator.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Pursuing a private summons will require the victim to spend time, effort and costs without Police assistance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: VCH is a common offence that occurs daily.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a large number compared to other reported offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the total crimes recorded last year was about 33,000 which, I believe, excludes the 10,000 VCH reports.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The figure of 10,000 cases is also likely to be an underestimate, as many cases go unreported.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of the 10,000 reported cases, only about 600 resulted in criminal charges being filed, a rate of about 6%.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: PCRC is right to note that some past scenarios of VCH can, in fact, be quite serious.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In some cases, the injuries may be permanent; there may be elements of bullying or of being outnumbered by a few assailants.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Accordingly, I am supportive of the introduction of section 323A to create a new offence of causing grievous hurt even though only hurt was intended.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will now be an arrestable offence attracting higher punishment of up to five years' jail, which the Police will be empowered to investigate without a Magistrate’s order.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, the Committee rightly pointed out that some victims may sustain injuries which are serious and yet do not fall within the definition of grievous hurt, for example, multiple injuries caused in a prolonged attack.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill’s response to this is to raise the maximum imprisonment for VCH itself from two years to three years, but to continue to keep it as a non-arrestable offence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was stated in the PCRC Report that the need for a Magistrate’s complaint would ensure that only meritorious cases were investigated by the Police.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Report further emphasised that the Police did itself take the initiative to investigate and prosecute in the “egregious” cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What kinds of scenarios have resulted in the Police initiating investigations and prosecutions without a Magistrate’s complaint being filed?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How are VCH cases currently triaged for action or non-action?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, did most victims expect the Police to take some action?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From time to time, VCH victims express surprise and disappointment that the Police are not taking up their complaints.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, does the Ministry not acknowledge that relying on victims to file a Magistrate’s complaint requires victims to have the resources and a certain fortitude to navigate the legal system on their own?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is probable that this requirement to see a Magistrate may not necessarily flag out the most meritorious cases, but cases with the most determined victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The changes proposed in the Bill to create the new section 323A and to increase the maximum punishment for section 323 are improvements and will facilitate more robust responses to the more serious VCH cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, the situation needs further clarification and further monitoring to ensure that members of the public get justice for hurt offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this Bill, there are particular groups of victims deemed as vulnerable and in need of extra protection.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These groups are children under 14 years of age, domestic workers, vulnerable adults and victims in intimate or close relationships.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am concerned about what this caveat means and how it would potentially undermine the extra protection that was intended.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To be more explicit: in what way could it be shown that a domestic worker, a dementia patient or a child under 14 was capable of protecting themselves as any ordinary person?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clarification on this point would be most instructive.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, while the Penal Code may be amended to enhance punishments, it would be far better if the provisions were not invoked but, instead, achieve the goal of general deterrence, that is, to prevent incidents from happening in the first place.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, what plans does the Government have to publicise these changes, either to the general public, or in a targeted manner?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill introduces new offences to protect those above 16 but below 18 years, if the accused was in a relationship with the victim that is defined as, I quote, an “exploitative relationship” under the new section 377CA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is an important signal to parents, stepparents, guardians and other persons who are able to exercise some control or influence over the minor not to take advantage of young persons below 18.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Protecting minors under 18 is consistent with the United Nations (UN) Convention on the Rights of the Child which Singapore has signed and ratified.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this connection, I would like to clarify the amendments being proposed to the Children and Young Persons Act (CYPA).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under clause 171 of the Bill, enhancements are being made to protect children and young persons from being ill-treated and from being sexually exploited.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MSF recently conducted a public consultation and intends to table the change later this year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not know whether I heard him correctly and he may correct me if I am wrong.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But I understood him to be suggesting that certain tools be given to the Government to react quickly to emerging crime trends and one of the examples he gave was that, for example, CBT, as an agent, the Minister should be enabled to gazette new categories of relationships that would come within section 409.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am not sure whether I heard him correctly, perhaps he could clarify that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In fact, in the City Harvest case, the Court of Appeal made quite clear that there is need for reform but that it should be left to Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I hope the Member is not suggesting that Parliament relinquish its responsibility and delegate to the Minister such vast powers to create new criminal conduct.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, if you have any clarifications.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And I never asked for it to act retrospectively.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, I am looking at possibilities to make the system deter future activities through a more flexible use of legal tools.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Speaker, I would like to clarify that I know that he is not making a suggestion about retrospective laws.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: That would be against the Constitution in the first place.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But what I am expressing concern about is that I do not know whether he is suggesting that the Minister be given powers, even prospectively, to gazette new offences, new categories of offences that would come within certain sections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I mean, is the Member saying that MHA is too cautious to have this Bill to spell out certain categories and the Minister should be allowed to gazette new categories as and when he thinks it is necessary?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That was not what I said in my speech.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope it only means that more are seeking help.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is a basic human right to live in safety and freedom, free of fear from others.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Those who deny others this right must be severely dealt with.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill comes shortly after the Vulnerable Adults Bill was passed last year.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is a testament to the Government’s resolve to protect victims against perpetrators of abuse.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Aside from criminalising and penalising abusive behaviour, we need to continue working hard on preventive measures.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The man was jailed for six weeks for punching the maid.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why did they treat another fellow human being in such a despicable manner?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Has any research been done on this to see how we can correct such behaviour and get them to attend some rehabilitation while under detention?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What is being done to ensure that their attitude is corrected?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This includes not just abusers, but abettors and those who repeatedly witnessed the abuse but did nothing.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We also need to look out for those who fall through the cracks.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Such examples would include elderly and mentally-disabled people who are confined at home all day and less-educated foreign domestic workers who do not have a social network here and are confined to working at home most of the time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Also, some victims of domestic abuse refuse to seek help because they do not want the abuser to go to jail which, they feel, will bring shame on the family.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, we all need to look out for possible abuse cases amongst us and help the victims who might not want to seek help.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, I asked in Parliament how MSF can better assess risks of domestic abuse.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I shared that, in the United States (US), data analysis programmes help to identify the risks, complementing case workers' judgement.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is this something we can explore with data analytics technology?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Also, when people call helplines asking for help for issues like addictive behaviour or family disputes, should we proactively check if there is domestic abuse?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After all, these are often factors related to domestic abuse.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: While we are on the subject of domestic abuse, I would like to pledge my full support for the removal of marital immunity for rape.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A marriage is a union of two individuals and these individuals' personal rights should continue to be preserved and respected.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Non-consensual sex is rape and it must be treated as such.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I acknowledge the concerns about difficulty in proving consent, or lack of, between a married couple, and this law may even be abused when parties are negotiating a divorce, for example.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the authorities elaborate on how they intend to navigate this challenge?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am also glad to see that the Government is doing more to criminalise any action that could lead to sexual trauma to children, including exposing minors to pornographic material.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why are some minors on dating websites or open to dating adults?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What are the underlying issues and can we do something about it?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There were also incidences whereby the minor initially rejected the predator's sexual advances but still gave in to requests to send nude pictures or even met up with the predator, which then leads to rape.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am very worried for our young girls and boys who put themselves in such dangerous situations.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is there a lapse in our sex education programme?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Child sex predators have taken the form of neighbours, family friends, mother's boyfriend, son or relative of someone close.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In cases where parents have clearly disregarded their child's safety and also when they ignore their child's claims of sexual abuse or clear signs of it, some action should be taken to haul up the parents or guardian for failing in their duty.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When someone has been the victim of a peeping tom, it is bad enough.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But if a video taken by the peeping tom goes online, then the victim probably feels hurt all over again every time someone watches the video.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As I have said in my Parliamentary Questions, I hope we can have a public campaign telling people it is immoral and illegal to forward or watch such videos.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Whether it is peeping tom or other sexual offences, the Police should go all out to find the person.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And the same principles should apply, no matter where the crime was committed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Offenders should be dealt with strictly and tougher action is to be taken.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should send a strong signal that we have zero tolerance for sex harassment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The aim of this amendment Bill is to better protect those who are more vulnerable, to ensure that nobody will suffer from fear and is able to enjoy freedom.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have a few suggestions regarding how we can achieve this aim.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But while we punish them for their actions, can we also look into why they have such a disturbing mentality and how can we help them change that mentality?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And those who do nothing despite being aware that abuse is taking place, should also go for counselling and should even be punished.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What can we do to better detect these cases?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, with regard to sexual harassment of our youths, how can we educate youths to refrain from discussing sex with strangers so as not to put themselves at risk?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Fourthly, voyeurism on campus have been widely reported in the media recently.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that regardless of where these crimes take place, the Police will take a serious view in investigations and punish the perpetrators severely.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should not tolerate sexual harassment at all.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As Thomas Jefferson said, "Laws and institutions must go hand in hand with the progress of the human mind".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I will be addressing three areas of the law reform today.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The purpose of these sections is clearly to recognise the systemic vulnerability of certain victims and, therefore, the need for commensurate enhanced punishment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Similar wordings appear in the proposed subsections 74A(2A), 74B(3), 74C(3) and 74D(3) found in clause 18 of the Bill In practice, this provision could potentially require the victim to prove that he/she could not have done more to protect himself/herself.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There are sadly enough cases of domestic worker abuse.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One employer was charged last year for having punched her domestic worker so much over the course of a two-year period such that the latter had become blind in her left eye in addition to suffering from an injured right eye.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I do, however, believe that this should be removed as it inadvertently leads to harsh scrutiny of a victim's actions which encourages a culture of victim-blaming.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My Speaker, equally important to the continued protection of vulnerable persons and groups are that of education and raising awareness.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I would like the Minister to clarify on the Ministry's efforts to work with relevant community partners, such as schools, employment agencies and family service centres, to train and raise awareness on the new laws and the additional protection offered to the vulnerable that they support.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We are sending a strong signal on where we stand as a society with protecting and advancing women's rights.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is a significant change because it acknowledges that men can be the victims of sexual harassment and assault, too.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Not only will male survivors be able to seek legal remedy under this new definition, but this also implicitly acknowledges the unique struggles and social stigmas that male survivors face.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As a society, we should move towards destigmatising issues related to sexual assault and provide more support to all survivors, regardless of gender.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The PCRC decided against making changes to section 90, citing its general ease of application in Court.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I understand the Committee's concerns and acknowledge from the briefing notes on this Bill that the Government intends to create a new section to set out types of misconceptions of acts that will vitiate consent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, I am concerned that these measures might be insufficient in addressing the problem at hand.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, I know of such a case cited by the Association of Women for Action and Research's (AWARE's) SACC.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A survivor initially consented to have sex but later withdrew her consent when she realised that the man was too drunk and was being verbally abusive.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, she eventually complied with his demands for her own safety.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When she went to the Police, she was told multiple times, and I quote, "(but) you did consent initially".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This discouraged her from formally making a report as she felt she had no case, which was inconsistent with the precedents set by case law.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Case law presents a different, yet more straightforward, definition of consent compared to what is currently defined in the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It covers a number of situations where consent is negated.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, the definition of consent as developed by case law is not codified nor easily accessible.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I recommend that we adapt Ratanlal and Dhirajlal's definition of consent, which was referred to in Pram Nair v PP (2017).

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For ease of reference, the proposed specific definition of consent for sexual activity should be created under "Sexual Offences" of chapter 16 in the Code and should be defined as, I quote: "Consent is the free, informed and voluntary participation in the sexual activity in question.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lack of resistance and submission to sexual activity, in itself, is not consent as a matter of law." This encompasses the elements of free exercise of choice, voluntary participation and the exercise of choice based on the knowledge of the significance and moral quality of the act.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I also propose that the Government include a section to set out six specific situations where either there is no consent in law, or no consent is obtained.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Situation one, where the consent to participate is expressed under fear of injury or wrongful restraint to the person, or to some other person, including the accused.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Two, where the consent is given by a person who, from unsoundness of mind, mental incapacity, intoxication, or the influence of any drug or other substance, is unable to understand the nature and consequence of that to which he gives his consent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Three, where the consent is given by a person who is under 16 years of age.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Four, where a person says or does something to show that they are not willing to continue an activity that has started.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Five, where the accused causes or induces the complainant to participate in the activity by abusing a position of trust, power or authority.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One could argue that this is already recognised in the proposed section 375(3)(c) on exploitative relationship but that is only for minors.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: An exploitative relationship can also be a superior coercing his subordinate at the workplace into sexual activity.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Six, where the consent is expressed or implied by the words or conduct of a person other than the complainant.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This scenario would be applied to situations that SACC has come across where a wife’s consent is assumed if her husband told another man that he can have sex with her.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Sex education programmes need to explicitly discuss the meaning of consent and what it means in practice.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, I would like to comment on the decriminalisation of suicide, an issue very close to my heart, given the people I know around me, far and near, who have contemplated and attempted suicide.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill offers us, as a society, an opportunity to break the stigma by having a national conversation about it so that more can come forward to seek help.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The number of elderly aged 60 and above who took their own lives peaked in 2017, the highest since suicide tracking started in 1991.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, Mr Speaker, we must delink the convenient and linear association between suicide and mental illness.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Many studies have conclusively absolved mental illness as the only cause of suicide.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There are two other risk factors that make up the other 38%.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, for the young, life events like relationships, academic stress, National Service; for the elderly – bereavement, debt, feeling lonely and fear of being a burden; and for working adults – marital, financial, problems like unemployment or failed business, as well as legal problems.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The second risk factor is physical illness, another risk factor which means that suicides associated with physical illness, not unexpectedly, increase with age.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to, therefore, express my concern that the Police referring a person attempting suicide to a medical practitioner may inadvertently categorise all suicide attempters as having mental illness who need a medical “solution” and, as such, not be given the optimal and multifactorial approach he/she needs at that point of distress and after.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There were 361 suicides in 2017 according to SOS.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The latest number for attempted suicides is not available.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But in response to a Parliamentary Question raised in 2015, MSF reported that there were about 1,000 cases of attempted suicide each year between 2010 and 2014.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Because suicide is a crime under section 309, reporting of suicide attempts is mandatory as provided for in the CPC.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This will not be required with the repeal.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The World Health Organization (WHO) urges society and the individuals themselves not to associate suicide with immorality but to approach it with compassion, which I completely agree.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It also said that decriminalisation reduces suicide rates.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, there have also been studies of seven nations, namely, Canada, England and Wales, Finland, Hong Kong, Ireland, New Zealand and Sweden, that present a contradicting conclusion where suicide rates were actually higher after decriminalisation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I reluctantly did a dip test with those around me who have contemplated or attempted suicide.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: None knew that committing suicide was a crime in Singapore at that point of their attempt and most added that it would not have deterred them even if they had known it was.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I am also not convinced of the deterrent effect of section 309 in preventing suicides.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must do more to raise awareness of suicide risk factors, shift perceptions on mental health and deepen community-based efforts in active monitoring, reporting and help-seeking.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must do more to counter the threats of rising suicides amongst our young and elderly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the wider use of technology, changing social norms and an evolving crime and criminal environment, it is timely and imperative to review and amend the Penal Code to ensure our criminal laws serve to deter and prevent crime.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I will focus my speech on the new offences relating to voyeurism, crimes against children and a few other provisions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Rapid technological advancements have led to the development of sophisticated devices and equipment that a perpetrator could easily manipulate to record private acts and distribute recordings of such acts or images of the victim.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The recent cases at our university's halls of residence are a timely reminder and further impetus for our laws to keep pace in tackling the rise of such criminal behaviour.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The current law is inadequate to address the problems brought about by advancements in spy and hidden camera technology.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The prosecution had to resort to the Films Act and section 509 of the Penal Code to take action against the perpetrator.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, I am concerned that the offence might be too broad as to criminalise private investigators in the course of their work, or witnesses trying to make a recording for the purposes of reporting a crime, or caregivers checking on the safety of their charges.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Whilst it is acknowledged that the new provisions to criminalise such offences are progressive and keep pace with the changing modes of commission of such offences, it cannot be denied that there is sometimes little comfort to the victims to have the perpetrators punished.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The pivotal concern of the victim, especially the more vulnerable minor and young person, would be to have those images or recordings deleted immediately and to prevent further distribution.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The laws and processes need to address this.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the same vein, punishment of the perpetrator for the offence of possessing or distributing voyeuristic, intimate images or recordings might not end the distribution chain.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is suggested that the perpetrator be compelled by law to disclose the source from which access to the images or recordings was gained.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This would enable the law enforcement agencies to trace the original source of the offending act and take the necessary action against the original perpetrator which would prevent the further distribution of the images or recordings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On the other side of the equation, the perpetrator should be helped and treated since voyeurism is often associated with a recognised psychiatric disorder.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Courts could be empowered to refer the perpetrator, upon the assessment of a psychiatrist, to psychiatric treatment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The appropriate punishments, coupled with psychiatric treatment, could well minimise recidivism.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The global market for child abuse material is growing at an alarming speed, "aided" by advances in technology and the World Wide Web.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, this is an offence only if the minor and the perpetrator are in an exploitative relationship.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is a defence, by virtue of section 377BM, where the accused person is able to prove that he did not intentionally come into possession of or gain access to the intimate image or recording and, on becoming aware that he has in his possession or he has gained access to the intimate image or recording, he has, as soon as practicable, taken all reasonable steps to cease possession of or access to the intimate image or material.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The same defence, by virtue of section 377BN, is available to an accused person charged with the offence of having possession of or gaining access to child abuse material under section 377BK.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For the same reasons mentioned earlier, it is suggested that the accused be compelled to disclose the source from which he obtained or gained access to the offending material.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Whilst it is agreed that a tough stance ought to be adopted in the punishment of perpetrators in order that minors below 14 years of age could be protected, it must be noted that punishment alone would not deter or reduce such crimes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Education of minors is essential to enable them to recognise criminal acts against them and, just as essential, is that the minors must know where they can go to immediately for help and support.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Hence, a robust support system must be established and it is suggested that our schools step up their support system as teachers and school counsellors are usually who the minor will go to for help.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Perpetrators must also be given help and treatment, especially if they are serial offenders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In addition, a support system for perpetrators after their release from prison would help to prevent re-offending.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I applaud the enhancing of section 509 and making it gender-neutral to balance the protection of not just females but males as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Even as I support the decriminalisation of attempted suicide, I hope this move will not be counter-productive and result in more people tempted to this, but more support mechanisms from a whole-of-Government and a whole-of-community approach to helping those in need.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Outmoded offences have been removed whilst gaps in the law pertaining to new offences brought about by societal changes as well as the gaps in the law pertaining to minors and vulnerable persons have been addressed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The amendments and new provisions have also codified the law relating to offences which were previously defined by separate pieces of legislation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This Bill has addressed offences thoroughly and comprehensively at this point of time and will help ensure that Singapore remains as one of the safest and most secure countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Police investigators, law enforcement professionals, prosecutors, lawyers, doctors, psychiatrists, domestic helpers and the layman will be directly or indirectly impacted by these changes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I hope a thorough, concerted and multi-pronged approach be taken to cascade, inform and educate the categories of people outlined earlier, including potential complainants, perpetrators and the young in general, to better understand the plethora of changes and new provisions introduced.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With these submissions and suggestions, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 5.02 pm until 5.20 pm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The careful consultation process that led to this Bill started with the formation of PCRC in July 2016 and culminated in extensive public engagements after publication of the PCRC Report in September 2018.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This should be a model that any complex, far-reaching legislation should follow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I will speak on the relationship between the law and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If laws are not properly limited and implemented, the law may have significant unintended and adverse effects on social behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Less recognised is the fact that social standards also give the law effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Without a shared consensus around the justness of the law, victims will hesitate to seek justice and offenders will be emboldened.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: My concern on the unintended adverse effects of the law relates to this Bill's enhanced protection for vulnerable persons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill enhances criminal law around offences against vulnerable persons, in line with recent reforms, such as the Vulnerable Adults Act 2018.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Sections 335A and 335B make similar provisions for abuse and acts that endanger life or personal safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In last year’s debate on the Vulnerable Adults Act, many Members spoke on how vulnerable adults need the protection of the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What I want to clarify is how these increased protections in criminal law will sit with the rights of the vulnerable elderly to choose how to live out their days in the manner they consider the best.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the book "Being Mortal", American surgeon Atul Gawande reflects on the excessive focus that modern medicine places on prolonging life rather than on ensuring a high quality of life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Medical interventions towards the end of life often cause great harm to the dignity or autonomy of patients.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The patient must trade the comforts of home for endless nights and days in the intensive care unit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The patient must endure becoming dependent on others for every little aspect of daily living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The additional days or even weeks of life in this state are not always considered worthwhile.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Given these tradeoffs, many among the elderly, when faced with a medical emergency or a serious illness, may wish to avoid treatment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They will expect their families to interpret and act on their wishes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I want to be clear I am not discussing euthanasia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These are still very serious offences under the Penal Code.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But there is a wide range of practices at the end of life which are not euthanasia in the ordinary sense.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some practices are widely accepted, such as choosing to refuse resuscitation or artificial life support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These are codified in the Advance Medical Directive Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Others are more controversial, such as refusing nutrition, medication or medical advice and treatment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Consider some examples of decisions made by persons near the end of life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: End-stage renal failure patients may choose to stop dialysis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Patients with cancers and other diseases addressable through medical interventions often refuse treatment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The elderly may wish to stay at home, instead of going to the hospital when their health deteriorates significantly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Former US President George HW Bush, at the end of his life, informed his staff he did not want to return to hospital and, as a result, he passed on peacefully at home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What makes an otherwise accepted practice neglectful, given that there will be concerns about the mental capacity of vulnerable adults and their physical inability to seek treatment without the support of their family?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Which practices do we want to proscribe in the law?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If the law is written in the first chapter, then we can expect it will be used in the next.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Family members may disagree on the appropriate medical intervention for a gravely ill vulnerable adult and, if they cannot prevail in a discussion, they may consider involving the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A gravely ill vulnerable adult may lose autonomy in their decision to stop treatment, because the family is both concerned the adult lacks mental competence and the family fears breaking the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A healthcare or social work professional may refer a case to the Police because they believe the vulnerable adult or the family is refusing treatment so as to constitute neglect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There may be cases where the family does fail in its duty of care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, we do not want cases to be referred unnecessarily to the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Terry Schiavo case in the US created a protracted legal battle over the so-called right to die.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mrs Schiavo was in a persistent vegetative state and her husband, who was her legal guardian, argued she would have wanted withdrawal of artificial life support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The case was exploited for political purposes and resulted in a 15-year legal battle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This House has expressed grave concerns about the growing practice of defensive medicine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Given that aggressive medical intervention in the last stage of life is often futile, costly and harmful to the dignity and autonomy of the patient, we would not want such interventions to become routine simply because of legal precedent, or fears by medical professionals and family members about their potential legal liability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, I ask the Government to provide clarity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What is expected of the medical treatment of a vulnerable elderly adult near the end of life in the home environment?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To what extent can, or should, the wishes of the vulnerable adult be respected with regard to medical treatment and other acts that affect life?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, is it neglectful if the family does not convey a gravely ill vulnerable adult to hospital, because of their expressed desire to pass on at home?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What if the vulnerable adult wishes to stop routine medical medication and consultation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How can families assure themselves that their actions are lawful and in furtherance of the vulnerable adult’s wishes to live a good life until the end?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I note that the Minister for Social and Family Development touched on these issues in the debate on the Vulnerable Adults Act 2018, which also enhanced penalties for offences against vulnerable adults.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill, however, proposes specific sections of the Penal Code which may affect the autonomy of vulnerable adults and their families in making end of life decisions and so, should be addressed separately today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But I fear that enhancing these provisions against sexual offences may be meaningless if we are ultimately hypocrites as a society and we do nothing about the social norms that tolerate such behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The experience of many countries in recent years with the #MeToo movement is instructive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In many countries, there are already strict laws against sexual offences and sexual harassment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, despite decades of actively enforced law, we had the #MeToo movement, a grassroots movement by women fighting against sexual harassment as a daily fact of life that women felt they had to accept in order to progress in their chosen careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The law, in short, was not an effective recourse for many women around the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Nor did the law restrain the behaviour of many men.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: After she came forward, other women reported similar experiences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As Ms Monica Baey posted on Instagram on 1 May 2019, and I quote: "I hope that Singapore has reflected on what has happened, why this blew up as big as it did and learn not to avoid issues but rather face the hard reality – sexual misconduct and assault are much more prevalent than it appears to be." Sir, these revisions of the law are just a means to the end.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The social objective must be to create the conditions for a society where the law is rarely applied because all segments of society accept that these acts are wrongful and there are strong cultural and social norms against such sexual offences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The criminal justice system cannot undo the harms caused by a sexual offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The trauma of an offence will remain with the victim for life.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the Bicentennial Commemoration this year, I think it would be apt to pay tribute to the original framers of the Penal Code, which is one of the oldest pieces of legislation in Singapore, in the administration of criminal justice in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Prof Ho Peng Kee, the then Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs, colourfully described the Penal Code as "the mother of all statutes" when it was last reviewed in this House in 2008.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are masterful commentaries about the history of the Penal Code in two textbooks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first book is "The Criminal Law in Malaysia and Singapore" by Profs Stanley Yeo, Neil Morgan and Chan Wing Cheong.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Incidentally, Prof Stanley Yeo and Prof Chan volunteered as members of PCRC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The second book is "The Development of Singapore Law: Historical and Socio Legal Perspectives" by Prof Andrew Phang as he then was.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I relied on these commentaries in the preparation of my speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The principal framer of the Penal Code was Lord Thomas Babington Macaulay.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 1837, the Law Commission, which he chaired, produced the draft of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For the draft, Lord Macaulay drew inspiration not just from English common law but two other sources: (a) the French Napoleonic Penal Code of 1791 and (b) Livingstone’s Code for Louisiana which was printed in 1833.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He drew from the best ideas from continental Europe, America and the UK.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Already then, it was not uncommon to trawl the world for best ideas to be incorporated into draft legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Eventually, the Penal Code was introduced in India in 1860.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Since then, law students, lawyers and our Courts have referred to Indian case law when interpreting our Penal Code provisions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What were the main objectives of the Penal Code then?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The principal objective was to codify common law criminal offences, which are really judge-made law and, in the words of Prof Phang, "replace the manifold systems of criminal law then existing" with a single code.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Penal Code allowed lay people to understand what kind of action and behaviour amounts to criminal conduct as well as the precise ingredients that make up the offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Almost 150 years later, the Penal Code continues to play an important role in the administration of the criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Penal Code is applied every day in the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the evolving nature of our society and our mores, the Penal Code had to be, and indeed was, revised from time to time to ensure its relevance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As mentioned earlier by the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin, the last revision of the Penal Code was done by this House a little over a decade ago in 2008.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have reviewed the work of the PCRC chaired by the hon Minister Indranee Rajah and co-chaired by Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The PCRC members are all eminent people drawn from the judiciary, legal service, Ministries, academia and private practice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Together, with their collective knowledge, experience and wisdom, they are uniquely well-placed to undertake the review.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As we heard from Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin, they delivered a 500-page tome.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe that this House owes the PCRC a debt of gratitude for executing the gargantuan task of updating the Penal Code so well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also commend MHA, just like what Assoc Prof Walter Theseira said, for conducting extensive consultation with the public and VWOs before presenting this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The recommendations that the Committee made took into account issues raised by our Courts in many judgments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am reasonably assured that, with these enhancements, the revised Penal Code, once passed, will continue to play an important role in the administration of criminal justice in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would now like to make several observations and comments on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also an offence to imagine the deposition of the President from the sovereignty of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It simply does not sit well with the mores and values of present-day society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am not alone in making this call.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Mr Charles Chong made this call in 2008 in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said, "It is, of course, right that anyone who plots, plans or actually takes action against the person or the Office of the President ought to be punished, but merely 'imagining' any of these – should this really be in our books?" It did not appear that Mr Charles Chong's question was answered then.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How does the narrowing of the definition of "criminal conspiracy" reflect on the expected sense of behaviour within our society?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How does this square with the retention of the offence of criminal defamation under section 500 of the Penal Code which focuses on vindication of reputation?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As Members know, people who have been defamed also have a right of civil action, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have also noted that, potentially, aggravated acts of defamation, such as "threats imputing the unchastity of a woman" under section 506 of the Penal Code, and "insulting the modesty of a woman" under section 509 of the Penal Code are proposed to be repealed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What then is the basis to continue to make defaming another a criminal matter in these circumstances?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would, therefore, take care of the concern expressed by PCRC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It allows the Police to intervene by arresting and sequestering the person in a safe environment, for example, a padded cell, so as to stabilise his or her condition.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand from Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin that it is proposed that the Police be given powers to intervene.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I seek a clarification on the basis and extent of these powers, as well as when it is expected for these Police Officers to be vested with such powers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next point, I believe there is a basis to consider amalgamating Penal Code provisions which cover the same ground as provisions in specific pieces of legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will allow for a more uniform application of the law dealing with the same area.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, reforms of these areas can be done more quickly, instead of waiting for the next review of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I commend the move to transfer the Chapter XX offences dealing with "offences relating to marriage" to the Women’s Charter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Similarly, the Penal Code provisions dealing with kidnapping could have been consolidated with the provisions in the Kidnapping Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This also would be an opportunity to deal with and remove an anomaly in sentencing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Kidnapping under the Kidnapping Act may be punishable by death.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not the case in Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, the corruption offences vis-a-vis "public servants" in the Penal Code could be merged with the Prevention of Corruption Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I seldom hear of these provisions in the Penal Code being invoked nowadays.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Again, the Penal Code punishment for corruption offences is lighter than the Prevention of Corruption Act equivalent.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: These also include charging members of the household guilty of offence for causing or allowing the death of a child under the age of 14.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: While we have a comprehensive, robust Bill to protect victims from criminal offenders, it is contingent upon us to constantly look for ways to facilitate the reporting of domestic violence.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The reasons for not reporting can be complex as they range from social, psychological and financial considerations to the ease of reporting.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: A quote from social workers from a Straits Times' article in 2017 has indicated a disparity where, "when a child is abused by a stranger, family members are quick to report; however, this is not so when the abuser is a family member." In recent years, there has been a trend of cases involving children dying or severely traumatised from brutal, chronic physical, psychological and sexual abuse in households.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: And to hear of this is absolutely heart-breaking.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It is also very distressing that most child abuse cases in Singapore involve caregivers.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In 2015, MSF was quoted by The New Paper stating that "in the 64 cases of alleged sexual abuse reported and investigated from January to September 2015, for every case, the alleged perpetrator was a family member or someone residing in the same household as the victim." These cases often go unreported as the victims are afraid that the family may be devastated.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The victims, more often than not, are unable to fend for themselves or are too afraid to come forward to seek help.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As such, it is of paramount importance that members of the public, such as the neighbours, relatives and friends, are encouraged to come forward to identify victims of family violence.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In a similar vein, spouse abuse is the most common form of family violence in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Concurrently, a standalone app or feature should be introduced like our current municipal app, such as OneService or SG Secure, to handle all social abuse ranging from child, spouse, elderly or other vulnerable groups and even include animal abuse to allow for a more coordinated response.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This way, victims do not have to be routed to call various touchpoints and repeat their accounts.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This dedicated hotline and app can be designed to offer all victims of domestic abuse immediate relief from their plight in three stages: firstly, through crisis intervention and counselling; next, indoctrination and action on the various channels of recourse; and consequently, a successful resolution and rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Our current system requires victims to call various resources at different hotlines, which is confusing and can be a deterrent.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The staff working at this central hotline and app can be trained in crisis intervention and be assigned to handle individual cases to build rapport with victims through counselling.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: They can then coordinate with local resources, such as the Police, hospitals, or pro bono legal aid for a more integrated, victim-centric care.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The staff can then work out a personalised safety plan, which will include how to receive financial assistance and how to gather evidence of abuse if the case goes to Court.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In the event that the victim cannot continue residing in their home for fear of continued abuse, coordinating staff will assist to put them up in a temporary shelter and seek protection order on their behalf with their consent.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Victims can also be directed to websites, such as AWARE, through the app, where information on domestic violence education can be found.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This is if they feel the need to consider their situation before taking further action.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It is also vitally important that an algorithm be implemented in the app to separate the more urgent cases and triage victims who require immediate medical attention from abuse.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Through these processes, victims will be able to chart their journey towards restitution and rehabilitation should they choose to lodge a formal report.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: They will also be educated on frequently asked questions and fully assured that there will be no backlash from their abusers.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: There have been many precedents where victims have successfully sought recourse through lodging a report, and these inspiring stories should be made aware through the app to encourage reporting.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This central hotline and app can also be a platform for members of the public or bystanders to report abuse cases with anonymity, and an avenue where they can be taught how to help victims of abuse.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: However, while most do not report such cases to the authorities or hotlines, many may want to seek advice or information for family members or friends.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Having a standalone app or a secondary municipal app feature will be useful in encouraging reporting or seek information on how to help abuse victims.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Members of the public may be more comfortable making a report online compared to calling a hotline.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: There are many examples of such apps available overseas and their features which can be used as reference.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The Daisy app in Australia provides information about support services within the vicinity and includes safety features to help protect the privacy of people using it.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In the US, the Sojourner Peace app is available in multiple languages and provides resources for victims of domestic abuse in a quick and discreet way.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It also provides links and phone numbers to places where survivors can seek help and access the Sojourner's 24-hour domestic violence hotline.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my above points, I stand to support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The proposed comprehensive amendments to the Penal Code are timely and will serve to ensure that our laws remain relevant in the new digital era.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to seek clarifications on some parts of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, I strongly support the proposed amendment that targets voyeuristic activities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As MHA and MinLaw have noted, there is a bustling online marketplace for upskirt photographs and videos.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, the current law we have is inadequate to address the problems brought about by the advancements in micro camera technologies and the prevalence of such cameras to the general public.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is a need for targeted laws to outlaw the act of observing or recording a person without their consent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But while this will serve to protect victims of voyeurs, some private investigators (PI) have expressed concerns.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How would they be impacted by this new offence?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the PIs continue to conduct surveillance operations to collect evidence for their clients?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I am in full support of the repeal of marital rape.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Married women should have the same access to protection as unmarried women.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But there remain practical challenges in implementing this.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of my residents have also spoken to me to voice concerns over potential false allegations of rape by an estranged spouse.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask what safeguards there are to ensure such allegations are carefully dealt with.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Notable cases in recent years have made this change necessary.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In 2016, two-year-old Mohamad Daniel Mohamad Nasser died after five weeks of abuse by his mother and her boyfriend.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In 2017, a couple tortured 26-year-old waitress Annie Ee Yu Lian who had intellectual disabilities for eight months.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In both cases, the victims were vulnerable and abused by their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While this deterrent will provide greater protection to vulnerable people by putting the onus on witnesses to report the abuse, what if the witness was also a victim of abuse, either mentally or physically, by the perpetrator?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, take the case of a mother who is a victim of abuse herself and, out of fear, she did nothing to stop the abuse to her child.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note that this was a recommendation by the PCRC, which was of the view that raising the minimum age would not be a significant risk to public safety.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While this change might seem reasonable if we compare the minimum age to global benchmarks, I have my concerns and ask that we could perhaps also look at things in a local context.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Locally, we are experiencing an increasing trend of reported cases of children beyond parental control (BPC).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The ages of these children are also getting younger.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: According to recent reports by MSF, we are also seeing BPC cases involving children 10 years old and younger.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my previous life as a Police officer, I was always concerned to see young offenders, especially who were still in primary schools.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I worry that it would lead to a phenomenon where unruly, unsupervised young children can possibly commit crimes without liabilities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to pay close attention to young at-risk children, as well as the number and age of young offenders arrested for crime.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More importantly, are there plans to effectively arrest the trending increase of BPC cases?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, the proposed amendments to the Penal Code have generally resulted in increases to the maximum jail sentences.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would possibly lead to a corresponding increase in jail time meted out to offenders.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What would be the impact on our prisons, and does our Prison Service have the resources, both in terms of infrastructure and manpower, to support this?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The amendments are essential to ensure that our Penal Code continues to remain relevant in today’s context.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to thank the men and women in the PCRC for the hard work put in over more than two years to put together this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Allow me to begin my speech in Malay.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   A few years ago, we were jolted by the news about the death of Ms Annie Ee, an intellectually disabled person who was abused, tortured and punished by her housemates.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many people condemned the heinous acts inflicted on Annie, especially in view of her condition which made her more vulnerable to abuse, and those who committed those acts were people who were close to her.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: After the Court case ended, many felt that the sentence imposed was not commensurate with the crime.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At that time, many asked why the couple who committed the offences were not charged with murder.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The couple had pleaded guilty to various charges of causing grievous hurt.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The current legislation requires the prosecutor to prove that the final action committed had led to death.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This was difficult to do when the torture took place over a long period of time.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Another case that jolted Singaporeans was the one where there was abuse inflicted on a toddler, Muhamad Daniel Muhamad Nasser, who was only two years old.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He was kicked and slapped by his mother and her boyfriend almost every day and forced to eat dried chillies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The toddler eventually died due to head injuries.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These cases shake us to the core as human beings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These people who commit atrocities on defenceless victims deserve a heavier punishment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is a reflection of our principles as a society to strongly condemn inhumane actions towards those who are vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Over the past several years, we seem to see several cases involving victims who are unable to defend themselves and the current punishment do not appear to be commensurate with the heinous crimes inflicted on the victims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Something needs to be done, and I am glad to see proposals within this Bill that increase the punishment on those who abuse and torture defenceless victims who are unable to defend themselves because of their own condition and also because they have close relations with the perpetrator.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are also suggestions for a new type of offence for abuses that lead to the victim’s death.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is a good thing and I support the recommendations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): When people first heard about what happened to the late Annie Ee, there was condemnation against the heinous acts carried out against her.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: When people heard about the charges and the punishments imposed on the perpetrators, many voiced out their concerns that the punishments were not commensurate with the severity of the crime and the fact that Annie was especially vulnerable as she was intellectually disabled.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In Annie’s case, the perpetrators eventually pleaded guilty to various counts of causing grievous hurt and causing grievous hurt with a weapon.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Cruelty against vulnerable individuals particularly offends our sense of morality as the victims are helpless and their ability to protect themselves is limited.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: To quote the PCRC, society reserves "special disapprobation" for the abuse of vulnerable people by their caregivers or others in a position of trust.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There must, therefore, be appropriate and commensurate penalties against offences of such nature.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am, therefore, supportive of the proposed enhancements of the penalties for offences against vulnerable persons in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that in the wake of Annie Ee's case, the public also reflected on how such a prolonged abuse could have taken place with no one reporting the same to the authorities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Vulnerable Adults Act, which was the outcome of, and was in response to, various concerns regarding abuse against vulnerable adults which had been raised even preceding Annie Ee's case, also took into account recent cases and allowed for more detection of abuse and protection for the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, I would like to seek clarification on the difference between the definition of "vulnerable person" in this Bill and "vulnerable adult" in the Vulnerable Adults Act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe a clarification may aid in the future applications of both pieces of legislation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Clause 83 of this Bill seeks to introduce new sections 304B and 304C to the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The new section 304B relates to causing death of a child below 14 years of age, domestic worker or vulnerable person by sustained abuse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The new section 304C relates to causing or allowing the death of a child below 14 years of age or vulnerable person in the same household.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note the distinction made between the two new sections.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate and thank the Minister for the clarification.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Criminal Law Reform Bill seeks to amend the Penal Code and bring it up to date.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Penal Code, as mentioned by many colleagues, is an important piece of legislation in Singapore, as it consolidates laws that relate to criminal offences.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: First enacted as the Straits Settlements Penal Code in 1871, the Act has been reformed on numerous occasions to bring it up to date.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In recent decades, in 1973, there were enhancements of punishments to curb the use of violence by criminals; in 1984, the introduction of more deterrent punishments for certain offences; in 1998, the enhanced punishments for abuse of domestic helpers; and in 2008, a decade ago, amendments to expand the scope of offences.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, we are making important amendments to the Code.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is the result of two years of discussion by PCRC.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: After the recommendations, there was engagement with more than 700 stakeholders and with submissions from over 60 individuals and organisations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I applaud the committee and the Ministry for undertaking this much needed review.
