speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There has been robust consultation, and the taking on board of suggestions and feedback.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the Bill involves many changes which many of my hon colleagues have already covered, I will confine my speech to two particular areas which I had previously raised in this House.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In May 2016, I highlighted that our current penal code is not gender-neutral and made a request to the Ministry to consider reforming our Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This was in relation to the April 2016 case of PP vs Zunika Ahmad.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this case, she was acquitted by the High Court of six charges under section 376A(1)(b) of sexually penetrating a 13-year-old in a landmark decision.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The case was subsequently heard in appeal before the Court of Three Judges.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The apex Court overturned the High Court decision.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The hon Chief Justice emphasised that section 376A was to be gender-neutral.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It also expands protection to cover a victim that is an adult male who is forced to engage in penetrative sex against his will by a female perpetrator.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This brings the statutes up to date and affords men, especially juveniles, protection.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We do not as yet have such confusion in our laws that have led to unbelievable circumstances elsewhere, such as in the 1993 case heard before the court in Kansas in the US.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Hermesmann vs Seyer was a pivotal case in the US, where a woman convicted of statutory rape of a minor and was pregnant as a result of the act, later successfully sued to claim child support from her victim.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is hoped that such a situation would never arise in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Second, with regard to Child Abuse Material, I raised a question in April 2017 to ask if the Minister for Home Affairs will introduce specific laws on child pornography.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am glad that the public consultations show broad support to criminalise non-fictional child abuse material.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, child abuse material should be abhorrent in whatever form it takes, whether it is non-fictional or fictional, and I would add, whether it involves a real child or a virtual one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The law seeks to recognise the special harm and depravity inherent in child abuse material and child pornography.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Criminalised NPPIC should include but not be exclusive to cartoons, animations and drawings, even if they are not indistinguishable that the child portrayed is real or fictional.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We will not be alone in this – sections 62-68 of the UK Coroners and Justice Act, sections 1466A(a)(1) and (2) of the US Protect Act, and section 1(17) of the Thailand Criminal Code Act.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child in relation to the sale of children, child prostitution and child pornography also refers to child pornography as any representation, by whatever means, of a child engaged in real or simulated explicit sexual activities or any representation of the sexual parts of a child primarily for sexual purposes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Sections 6(1) and (2) of the Undesirable Publications Act only imposes a conviction for a first offence to a fine of $2,000 to an amount not exceeding $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or three years.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The same is so for the Films Act.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The late Dr Victor Cline, who was Professor of Psychology, did an indepth research into sex addiction and pornography.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He describes four stages of sexualisation – addiction, escalation, desensitisation and actualisation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just earlier this afternoon, Minister Ong Ye Kung also alluded to the normalisation of behaviour with the availability of obscene material online.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In general, these amendments reflect sentiments on the ground.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The amendments have broadly enhanced protection for the vulnerable in society and tackles emerging crime trends.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I am glad our legal justice system is sufficiently nimble to move with the times and I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, there are a few sections which I have some concerns with.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In terms of trends, men accounted for over 66% of these deaths.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is the highest since suicide tracking started in 1991.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With the current Bill, section 309 of the Penal Code is repealed.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This means that attempted suicide is no more a crime.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We finally recognise that it is more important to rehabilitate and support those who want to commit suicide, rather than arresting and prosecuting those who have attempted suicide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As a Police officer in my younger days, I had attended to suicide cases as well as attempted suicide cases.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In one very memorable instance, I had to visit a young lady in the hospital after her second failed attempt at suicide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I had to record her statement and warned her that it was an offence to attempt suicide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She could not care less about what I said.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: A few days later, she made a third and final attempt, and was successful.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For people who are determined to end their lives, arrest and threat to charge her in Court is a poor deterrent to re-offending.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With that in mind, I would like to ask the Minister how many cases of attempted suicide were reported from 2010 to 2018.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Under the current law, abetment of suicide is a crime.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister how many cases of abetment of attempted suicide were reported from 2010 to 2018.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The above statistics are important for us to understand the underlying trends of suicide rate in Singapore and the effectiveness of our suicide prevention programme.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With the decriminalisation of attempted suicide, I hope that Government agencies will not trivialise the act of attempted suicide, especially if the Police are no longer involved or are playing a minor role.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope more resources, not less, will be channelled to help those who attempted suicide, more resources in terms of counselling to help the victim and victim’s families, more resources in terms of indepth studies on the causes of attempted suicide and suicide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is through this approach that we can better preserve the sanctity of life.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Perhaps we could look at what the Koreans have done.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Korea has one of the highest suicide rates in the world and the highest among the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: What the South Korean government did was to conduct an extensive study on 70,000 people who committed suicide from 2012 to 2016 to establish a National Surveillance System on Suicide Trend to analyse patterns and statistics on the causes of suicide and who is more likely to attempt suicide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It built strong local networks by educating medical and social workers on the ground so that they can immediately respond to those thinking of taking their own life.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It also strengthened depression tests to identify those who might be at risk.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We can take a leaf from Korea’s experience.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At the minimum, I suggest that we should mandate those who attempted suicide to go for counselling or treatment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For this to work, our anti-suicide effort needs to be an inter-Ministry collaboration, involving the Police, MSF and other stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Another area we have to be concerned about is teenage suicide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is particularly problematic because the youths are shockingly vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These youths and teens are increasingly at risk of self-harm due to bad influences through social media and challenges.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Such dark challenges could be disguised as a Momo Challenge, Blue Whale Challenge or hashtag #kys, that is, "kill yourself".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When the youths feel stressed, they can also easily go online to search for methods on how to kill themselves.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I hope that even with the decriminalisation of attempted suicide, the Police should not wash their hands completely.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Whenever there is such self-harm reported, the Police should still be alerted to rule out any abetment of suicide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Police can still be the referral agent to mandate Singaporeans who have attempted suicide to seek help.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Next, section 323 for voluntarily causing hurt (VCH).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The new section 323A fills in the gap between hurt and causing grievous hurt with intention.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Bill also enhances the punishment when hurt is inflicted on domestic workers, vulnerable persons and persons less than 14 years old.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, there is still a gulf between how the Police handle VCH cases and that of voluntarily causing grievous hurt.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: VCH under section 323 is a non-seizeable offence.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are many injuries which do not fall under "grievous hurt".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Grievous hurt relates to very serious injuries, such as fracture, blindness and other permanent disability.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Very often, "hurt" can be serious resulting in profuse bleeding, hospitalisation or a few days of medical leave.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Yet, it is still not serious enough to be classified as grievous hurt and the offence is not seizable.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The problem of a non-seizable offence is that the Police cannot make any arrest without a warrant.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The victim of VCH has to lodge a Magistrate's Complaint with the Courts.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is a onerous administrative process costing $20 and requires the victim to lodge the complaint personally in Court.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: He also has to buy a medical report from a hospital or clinic to state how he has been hurt.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Only when the victim of VCH has made a Magistrate's complaint that the Police will be directed by the Magistrate to investigate.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Hence, many perpetrators, many persons who try to hurt other people, get away quite easily.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the UK, you can get arrested for committing such offences.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Common assault, which includes pushing, slapping or merely spitting at people, such offences carry a maximum penalty of six months in prison.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Actual bodily harm, which is a step up, constitutes actual physical harm which does not need to be serious.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Actual bodily harm includes bruises, scratches and bite marks and the offence carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: How many cases were investigated by the Police due to Magistrate's complaint?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: How many cases were investigated by the Police without a complaint to the Magistrate?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: How many cases were eventually prosecuted in Court?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: One extreme is to follow the UK's example of making "VCH" to be a seizable offence.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I do not think the Police are ready for this.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the first place, there is no good reason for a person to assault another without provocation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Worse still, a customer service staff should not be assaulted by the very customer he or she is trying to serve.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If the Police can initiate investigations for such assault cases without the need for the victim to lodge a Magistrate's complaint, it will go a long way to deter such violent acts and bring justice to the victim in a fast, decisive and appropriate manner.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At this juncture, I would like to declare my interest as the Chief Executive Officer of ComfortDelGro Taxi Business before I continue my speech in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These were classified as causing hurt and not causing grievous hurt.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The majority of the victims could only look at the passengers going scot-free.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Currently, there is a huge difference between "VCH" and "voluntary causing grievous hurt".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The definition of "grievous hurt" includes serious injuries like fractures or blindness.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Even if the victim was badly beaten up and was hospitalised for a few days, he may not be considered as suffering from grievous hurt and the incident may not be investigated.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If he wants some form of justice, he has to pay for a medical report of his medical examination, take leave and pay another $20 to lodge a complaint at the Magistrate's Court.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For example, if the injury is serious enough to warrant more than one day of medical leave to recover, or if a customer beats up service personnel, the Police can investigate immediately and charge the perpetrators in Court.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I would like to continue my speech in English.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is good that we are finally repealing the marital immunity for rape, following the practice of other countries such as the UK, US and Australia.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We want to protect all women from sexual abuse, especially within the confines of their marriage, where they are most vulnerable and may find it difficult to say "no".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The amendment empowers them to step forward because a law has been broken.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, we do have to be careful to guard against false allegations of rape in instances where a married couple is not yet divorced, but the marriage has already broken down and the woman may want to "cry wolf" to fulfil a personal agenda.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Either that, or it could be a difference in interpretation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Using another context, there have been cases of women who claim that they were raped, but the men said that it was consensual sex.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Such charges are inherently based on "he says, she says", whereby it is quite impossible to obtain good evidence.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is challenging to prove a lack of consent in marital rape, due to the intimacy associated with marriage and the fluid nature of consent.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some even asked if a husband is supposed to get consent from the wife every time they have sexual relationships.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: A wife who consented may later retract it, in the heat of subsequent arguments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Will no signs of physical injury be sufficient to prove a false allegation of marital rape?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope the Minister can provide us with more insight.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the repeal for the immunity for marital rape restores dignity to women who suffered but were not accorded due justice.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Decriminalising attempted suicide while ensuring similar powers to require treatment marks a good balance between legislative powers and rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I remember rather vividly, as a young Police officer, I had to serve a warning to a young lady, paralysed from waist down, whose injuries were as a result of a failed suicide attempt.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Similarly, legislation against voyeuristic activities and revenge pornography reflects the tighter legislation needed for the digital age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Very frequently, our aged laws are not able to protect victims as technology progresses much faster than legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our law enforcement officers are often left with a patchwork of legislation across different statutes, stewing in their frustration to restore justice.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Left unaddressed, the digital world is no different from a crime-ridden ghetto where self-branded vigilantes prevailed and whose very inhabitants in this ghetto are also intimidated by these self-branded cops.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This set of Penal Code amendments will restore order and justice for many victims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Technological advancements meant that voyeurs are having their field days.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Armed with advanced zoom cameras, smartphones and insidious spying instruments, voyeurs make the world a very unsafe place, especially for women.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Not only do they not stop at filming or taking photos of very private moments, but they go on to upload and distribute on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, would private investigators also be prevented from taking such private videos even though it is presumably required in the course of their work?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As part of the amendments, the Bill also seeks to address the broad adverse impact from computer trading on the financial systems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because of the speed of trades, malicious and rogue traders can make a lot of money in a short span of time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They can also cause lasting damage and collapse financial systems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These amendments are important because of the growing number of financial fraud cases and the sophistication of the rogue traders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While I support the new sections to combat financial fraud, I have a few clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The latter requires that there must be wrongful loss or that there is a clear victim but not the new section.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While I note the need for a strong deterrence, can the Minister clarify why no victim is required as compared to the existing cheating offences?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I would also like to seek the Minister's clarification on the following.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, why is this new section needed instead of strengthening, for example, the Securities and Futures Act (Chapter 289)?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, the need for strong deterrence for financial manipulation is abundantly clear – the immense financial windfall breeds greed and might destabilise financial systems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Noting that the penalty is heavy compared to existing cheating offences, how is our regime compared with those of foreign legislation?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Were there previous cases in Singapore in recent years where we were unable to prosecute the perpetrator because there was no equivalent of a section 424A?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: According to section 424A(2), the new section 424A also does not require any of the three subsections, namely, section 424A(1)(a), (1)(b) and (1)(c) to be material for the offence to be made out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because the subsections need not have to be material and presumably more situations might be investigated under section 424A, under what circumstances does MHA envisage that such a piece of legislation would be used?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Third, what is the likely impact on the compliance requirements of our financial institutions upon the passing of this law?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Notwithstanding the above clarifications, I believe that this enhanced Penal Code will empower our law enforcers to protect us better.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This allows both Parliamentarians and the public to better understand and seek clarifications on such a crucial and comprehensive Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that this practice would be similarly adopted for other Bills which are equally important and extensive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to commend the progressive reforms this Bill introduces.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another applaudable aspect of this Bill is the PCRC's extensive efforts to obtain public input in this review.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Committee included leading practitioners and thought leaders from academia and the private and public sectors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To further strengthen this commendable effort at engaging the public, would the Government also consider including civil society groups on future review committees for any legislation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Civil society voices could have been especially value-adding and beneficial to the review process, given that many of these groups provide direct services and have expertise in the different issue areas subjected to review.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, these groups may have more experience dealing with certain groups of victims that avoid the authorities or are less inclined to report crimes and can provide valuable insights on these blindspots.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that it will become a standard practice for civil society to be included in committees spearheading legislative review rather than just at the consultation stage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This recognises that suicide attempts stem from deep-seated issues and a punitive approach may not be appropriate or sufficient in addressing them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond legislative reform, we can go further in addressing the needs of those who attempt suicide by ensuring that the authorities have the skills and resources to respond appropriately when these cases arise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Police officers are deployed when an attempted suicide case is reported.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Police officers are trained in responding to emergency situations but may not have sufficient training in handling the complex socio-emotional issues often associated with attempted suicide cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is considerable value in having trained professionals who can be at the scene to do any assessment on mental health or provide psychological interventions where necessary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similar trials have been conducted in the UK.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, will the Ministry look into improving the quality of response to attempted suicide by setting up a "specialist team with psychological first-aid training" that can be deployed when attempted suicide is reported?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, given that it may take time to train a specialist team, will the Minister consider deploying social workers, together with Police officers, when responding to attempted suicide cases?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would help ensure that there are experts on the scene who will be able to handle all aspects of the situation better.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, will the Ministry consider making it mandatory for frontline Police officers to undergo psychological first-aid training?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will ensure that the process is not as distressing for people who attempt suicide.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The MyResponder app works by notifying Community First Responders, who are members of the public trained in cardiopulmonary resuscitation or automated external defibrillator procedures, of nearby fire and medical cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The app could similarly notify trained social workers or counsellors who are available and in close proximity to the scene of attempted suicide cases so that they can assist the Police with negotiation efforts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister confirm if marital immunity for rape is completely removed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, section 376A penalises acts of sexual penetration against minors under the age of 16 but does not apply where there is spousal consent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, section 375(1) provides that penile-vaginal penetration of a girl under the age of 14 is rape but does not apply when there is spousal consent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The position is the same under the new section 375(1A) for oral or anal penetration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 376A(5) states that it is not an offence for a man to penetrate his wife if his wife is 13 years old and above.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that it is possible for a child between 13 and 16 years old who is in a marriage to give spousal consent to sex even though it would otherwise be considered as rape.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While this is a step in the right direction, would the Government consider further raising this minimum age to 12, in line with the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC)?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Paragraph 32 of the CRC recommends that states increase the MARC to the age of 12.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some have argued that logical thinking and problem-solving skills only develop between 11 to 15 years old.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some also suggest that intellectual abilities reach adult levels at only 17 years old.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Children with underdeveloped logical thinking, problem solving and intellectual abilities are more likely to exhibit risky and potentially criminal behaviour.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore’s Penal Code was enacted in 1871, a legacy of the colonial era.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It started as a codification of the criminal law for easy administration by Colonial officials in far out territories, many of whom would not be lawyers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While criminal law in England has not been codified in a single bill, the codification of the criminal law in the Penal Code has always been intended for the criminal law to be easily understood by a wider audience.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even a layperson reading the Penal Code would find the law clearly stated and helpful illustrations provided on how the law was to be applied.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, the Penal Code has undergone extensive changes over the last century and a half, and this latest set brings the Penal Code up to date with many of the latest developments in crime trends.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It also makes important changes to further protect vulnerable victims.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In making these changes, the Penal Code has retained the easy-to-understand drafting style that clearly sets out the offences and penalties involved as well as helpful illustrations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While the Penal Code itself is long, each of the offences is clearly set out and organised and a layperson should be able to understand the charges against him when charged for any of these offences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are important changes that recognise special vulnerability in these relationships.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All involve situations where one person is likely to be dependent on another or in a position of special trust with that person.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And the abuse of that special position by committing a crime, therefore, fully justifies a sterner penalty and sends the right signal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was a point that I and others in this House had raised on previous occasions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It has always been in my view a quirk of the law when it was argued a man could not rape his wife even if she did not consent to having sex with him.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of the reports of husbands abusing wives are particularly heinous, and while they may have involved sex forced through violence, the perpetrator could not be charged for rape but would often be charged with a lesser charge for the related violence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is also a series of offences that seem to be aimed at mischief that can have serious consequences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes making false reports of dangerous objects, such as declaring there is a bomb on the train when you know there is not one, causing or contributing to serious fire and this seems clearly to capture cigarette butts thrown down rubbish chutes that may cause fires.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is also criminalisation of negligence in respect of things like machineries tearing down buildings and even dangerous animals, which is fair because this makes it clear that people who have responsibility doing these tasks should take additional care.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are broad-ranging powers which criminalise not only the obtaining of such information but also those who gain access to it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I wholeheartedly support this reform and thank the Committee members for their hard work in putting these proposals together.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Members spoke positively about the amendments relating to vulnerable victims.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Members spoke eloquently and passionately about the need to protect the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Victims like Annie Ee and Daniel Nasser were mentioned in many of the Members' speeches.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: No words can express the sorrow their families went through.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We hope that the new laws protecting vulnerable victims will help to deter such cases from occurring.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked about the difference between "vulnerable person" in the Bill and "vulnerable adult" in the Vulnerable Adults Act (VAA).

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Hence, a narrow definition of "vulnerable adults" was adopted in VAA.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: This is to strike a balance between respecting individual autonomy and protecting those in need of help using intrusive protective measures.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Those that do not meet the high threshold in the VAA can and have been helped in other ways.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: This sends a strong deterrent signal and can potentially reduce the need to resort to intrusive remedial measures as envisaged in VAA.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We should give it time and MSF will keep a close watch to ensure the interests of the vulnerable in the community are looked after and the balance appropriately struck.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Mr Melvin Yong spoke about the proposed section 304 offence, and whether persons who are also suffering from abuse might be prosecuted for not taking action.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We have also provided that such circumstances include her past or present experiences of abuse as a result of an unlawful act by any member of the same household as her.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam also asked about the differences between the new sections 335A and 304C.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The bases for the introduction of these offences are quite different.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The offences of "failure to protect" has been proposed to cover persons who owe these vulnerable victims a duty of care.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: It reflects society's view that these people are responsible for the safety and well-being of the vulnerable victims in their care, custody or control.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The offence of "causing or allowing death" applies to members of the same household as, and who have frequent contact with, the victim.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: This offence was introduced to overcome an evidential difficulty where two accused persons who have the exclusive opportunity to harm the vulnerable victim deny any ill-treatment of the victim.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Ms Anthea Ong and Ms Sylvia Lim asked about conditions under which the Courts may apply enhanced penalties for the offences against vulnerable victims.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The enhanced penalties allow the Courts to punish offenders more severely if they prey on the vulnerabilities of certain persons.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: A person with a physical disability, for instance, may not necessarily be vulnerable, say, in respect of a white-collar crime like fraud.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There has to be a link between the vulnerability and the offence for enhanced punishments to apply.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Ms Irene Quay and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah made suggestions to improve the reporting and detection of domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Domestic abuse should, in the first instance, be reported to the Police.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Police are trained to deal with such cases and have the legal powers to intervene quickly to stop any imminent or ongoing abuse.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Police also work with MSF to ensure that the victim receives care and, if required, will physically separate the victim and the assailant.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: As Ms Irene Quay acknowledged, much has already been done by MSF.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked how the amendments relating to abuse and neglect of vulnerable victims interact with decisions associated with palliative care.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Bill does not affect bona fide palliative arrangements.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Bill, for example, at section 304C, introduces obligations on persons in the household who have frequent contact with the victim and who are aware of a significant risk of grievous hurt being caused to the victim to take steps which could reasonably have been expected of such persons to take, to protect the victim from the significant risk.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah spoke about rehabilitation of offenders in Prisons.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Psychiatric intervention will be provided to selected offenders where necessary and feasible.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Prisons' programmes also include psychology-based correctional programmes, family programmes and work programmes.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Patrick Tay suggested that psychiatric treatment or psychological counselling be mandatory for sexual predators after the completion of their sentence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Patrick Tay will be aware that offenders who are subject to the Mandatory Aftercare Scheme (MAS) for certain serious sexual offences are required to undergo community supervision and must comply with conditions, such as counselling and case management.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Melvin Yong spoke about the impact of the amendments on Prisons' resources.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Ministry will monitor the impact of the amendments on Prisons and continue to ensure that Prisons will be adequately staffed and resourced.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Members had a discussion earlier about the possibility of certain Penal Code offences being amended by Schedule.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: In general, Parliament should have oversight of criminal offences of general application, such as those in the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There is agreement that we do not retrospectively make acts criminal.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: On section 409, we acted to reform section 409 as quickly as practicable, considering the need to consult the relevant stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I believe that the amendment has benefited from Parliamentary scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: In the case of the Misuse of Drugs Act, it is a specialised legislation and the Schedule lists classes of substances.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: If we only list specific molecules, the peddlers will change one of many of the component molecules.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: So, there is, in that case, a particular operational context.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah spoke about minors dating adults and of dating websites.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We share Er Dr Lee Bee Wah's concerns and our response is multi-pronged.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The amendments today will deal with sexual exploitation of minors by adults.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We want to prevent predatory conduct by adults against minors.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We have also introduced a sexual communication offence to deal with sexting between an adult and a child.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We will closely monitor and take action against the users of dating websites or social media sites if they exploit young persons.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Alex Yam spoke on criminalising all forms of child abuse material.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The distribution and sale of fictional child abuse material are criminalised as "obscene material" in the Penal Code and will be subject to enhanced penalties.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We thank Mr Alex Yam for drawing our attention to the international developments and we will monitor the situation closely.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah spoke about cases where parents have clearly ignored the sexual abuse of their children.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: She asked about abettors and those who repeatedly witness abuse but do nothing.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The amendments criminalise the failure of caregivers to protect children from ill-treatment, which includes the subjecting of the child to sexual abuse.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the CYPA amendments, whether they will be brought into effect at the same time that MSF raises the proposed definition of "young person" to 18.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We will try to see whether we can have the changes take effect at the same time, or, if that is not possible, as soon as practicable.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Members supported the introduction of the new offence of voyeurism and distribution of intimate images.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Melvin Yong asked about the impact of the new offences of voyeurism and distribution of intimate images on private investigators, persons who report crimes, or caregivers.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There are defences where the recordings are for legitimate purposes.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Specific requirements apply to qualify for this defence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Among others, the act has to be done without malice, with reasonable cause and the image or recording is used for contemplated or pending Court proceedings and is not kept longer than necessary or required.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Desmond Choo sought a clarification on whether cases which involved the distribution of videos prior to these amendments coming into force would be investigated under the new offences.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: They would, if the distribution takes place after the provisions take effect.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: If their offending acts occurred before the new laws are in force, they would be dealt with under prevailing laws.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Patrick Tay also suggested that the Courts be allowed to make orders which essentially involve the deletion of the offending images or recordings.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Courts can order the disposal of any property which has been used in the commission of an offence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The CPC was amended last year to specifically allow an order for the deletion of data on a computer or mobile phone where the data was the subject of an offence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Patrick Tay also spoke on dealing with the source of the offending images.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The source of the images will be identified through Police investigations and the Police will do its best to track the source.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Those in possession of the images have to cooperate in investigations to provide information on the originators of such material.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah spoke about websites that carry prohibited material.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We take a strong stand against sites that host prohibited material.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) can issue directions to the Internet Service Providers (ISPs) to block access to such websites.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Internet content providers (ICPs) include web-hosting services, and they are all class-licensed under the Broadcasting Act.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: So, they are required to comply with the Internet Code of Practice and ensure that prohibited material is not hosted on their websites.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: If such websites are verified to be hosted in Singapore, IMDA can direct the ICPs to take down the content and suspend or cancel the class licences of the ICPs.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the extent of the repeal of marital immunity.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: His question also discusses sex within marriage involving minors.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: It is not tenable to completely ban minor marriages today.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: A majority of countries around the world share the same approach.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: First, all cases of alleged rape, within or outside of marriage, are subject to the same level of evidential rigour during investigation and prosecution.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Police officers at the Serious Sexual Crime Branch are trained to deal with complex issues of evidence and proof.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Second, there are existing offences in the Penal Code on false reporting and we are enhancing penalties for false reporting.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I want to thank Members for their support for the amendments to sections 375 on rape, 376 on sexual assault involving penetration, and 509 on insult of modesty.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Ms Anthea Ong supported the expanded legal definition of rape and spoke passionately about the need to protect all victims of sexual assault, regardless of gender.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Ms Anthea Ong spoke about a positive definition of “consent” in the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Instituting a new positive definition of consent could generate further uncertainty in view of the fairly settled law in this instance.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The PCRC studied this issue and found that the experience of England and Wales in having a positive statutory definition does not help in clarifying the scope of consent.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Ms Anthea Ong has suggested greater public awareness about the contours of consent.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We will work with agencies and organisations to improve on public education in this area.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Members spoke on the repeal of attempted suicide.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I was particularly struck by Mr Desmond Choo’s first-hand account from his days as a Police officer where he had to serve a warning to a semi-paralysed lady who had attempted suicide.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: With today’s amendments, such warnings will no longer be required.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Christopher de Souza set out his concerns regarding the decriminalisation of attempted suicide.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The abetment of attempted suicide is still a crime.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The amendments actually enhance the penalties for abetment of attempted suicide significantly.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Louis Ng spoke about support professionals that could assist the Police when intervening in attempted suicide cases.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Singapore Police Force's (SPF’s) Crisis Negotiation Unit is trained to handle cases like suicide attempts.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Comprising Police officers and psychologists, they are trained in negotiation tactics and suicide intervention.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Officers are also trained to ensure their own safety.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Social workers, for instance, at the Samaritans of Singapore (SOS) and Social Service Offices, can be involved later after the Police have ensured the safety of various parties.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We will look into Mr Louis Ng’s suggestion on psychological first aid training.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: On the use of MyResponder, interventions involving attempted suicide are different from CPR and AED procedures.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We want to avoid a situation where a well-meaning member of the public reacting to the notification exacerbates the situation or puts himself in a position of danger.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Murali Pillai spoke about Police intervention and treatment.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Where appropriate, the Police can still exercise powers under the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Act.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There will still be mental health treatment for appropriate cases.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: But as Ms Anthea Ong highlighted, not all cases involve mental illness.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: For others, counselling or family support may be needed.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Government will continue to maintain statistics, taking into account inputs from the various agencies which respond to suicide attempts.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Some Members have raised questions on whether decriminalisation will impact reporting by the public.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Our experience informs us that callers who call emergency lines to report attempts do not call to report a crime.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: They call for help, out of concern for the safety of the person attempting suicide and others in the vicinity of the person.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked for a study to be conducted following the decriminalisation.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We will monitor the situation post-amendment but we must remember that suicide attempts happen for various reasons.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: An increase or decrease in the number of attempts may not be attributable to criminalisation or decriminalisation.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked for statistics on reports for attempted suicide.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The medical literature suggests that there are multiple factors that affect suicide risk, ranging from barriers to seeking help, to economic downturns, to personal risk factors, for example, mental health disorders, substance abuse, financial problems and many others.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng suggested that there be mandatory counselling for those who attempt suicide.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: SOS operates a 24-hour hotline to counsel persons in distress.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Institute of Mental Health (IMH) operates a 24-hour Mental Health Helpline to assess and triage cases and activate home visit teams if necessary.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: To make it mandatory means that we will have to enforce the need to go for counselling and are likely to do so on pain of punishment.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Again, we are trying to move away, in this area, from criminalisation to help.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: So, we should tread carefully in this aspect.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Louis Ng spoke about the Minimum Age of Criminal Responsibility (MACR) and whether it could be raised to the age of 12.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There is currently no scientific consensus on what the MACR should be.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Persons of 10 years of age or above and under 12, can still avail themselves of a defence if they can show that they have not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of his conduct.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Melvin Yong spoke about his concerns regarding the raising of the MACR.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I hear the Member’s concerns, and assure him that the raising of the MACR will only come into force when the mechanism to address offending behaviour in children below the MACR is put in place.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The framework will ensure that children below the MACR will still have their behaviour addressed.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Both Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Ang Wei Neng spoke about VCH and arrestability.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: In addition, the expansion of the definition of “public servants” to include persons, such as those who conduct illegal parking enforcement on behalf of the Government, means that acts of hurt committed against a wider range of persons will be arrestable.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: So, we are moving incrementally, to ensure that cases get the appropriate response and there is no inadvertent diversion of Police resources away from critical cases.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about the various scenarios in which the Police initiate investigations for VCH cases without any Magistrate's complaint.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: These include acts of VCH which cause serious injury which falls short of grievous hurt; acts of VCH involved in road rage; VCH cases involving secret society members; racially or religiously aggravated VCH cases and acts of VCH against public service workers, such as taxi drivers, transport workers or nurses.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We will continue to monitor the situation with regard to VCH and study the various suggestions.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Post-amendment, we can assess if there is a need to create a more expedited framework for the resolution of other types of VCH cases and if this can be done without compromising due process or compromising the delivery of Police response to other more serious offences.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the proposed revision to criminal conspiracy.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There are no reported instances of the use of section 120A of the Penal Code against conspiracies to engage in non-criminal conduct.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There is no strong policy reason or public imperative to keep it in the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There is available recourse for such civil wrongs through the civil Courts.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The same approach is taken in the UK under the Criminal Law Act 1977, where criminal conspiracy is limited to agreements to commit offences.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: While there is civil recourse for defamation, the policy assessment is that there may be certain cases of defamation where criminal sanctions are required to reflect the seriousness with which society regards such conduct.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: It overlaps with a civil wrong, but so do other crimes, such as theft and fraud.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: A policy decision has been made for these acts to be treated both as crimes and as civil wrongs.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Murali Pillai has proposed moving the Penal Code offences relating to kidnapping or corruption to other specialised legislation.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We will consider Mr Murali Pillai’s feedback and will also ask the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau to consider it as well.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Member said there was an anomaly in sentencing, that kidnapping in the Kidnapping Act is punishable by death but this was not the case in the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The heavier penalties under the Kidnapping Act are due to the fact that kidnapping for ransom is involved.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Conversely, the kidnapping offence in the Penal Code encompasses a much broader range of conduct, including less serious conduct.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Desmond Choo sought clarification on the need for an identifiable victim for the new fraud offence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The LIBOR case is a clear example where dishonest gain can be made through the financial system without there being an identifiable victim or loss caused.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: It is very difficult to find a lay person who understands how LIBOR is calculated, given the arcane nature of the mechanism.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Proving loss is also extremely difficult, because LIBOR is an inter-bank lending rate and it only impacts ordinary consumers indirectly, and the impact depends on the practices of each bank, for example, in setting fixed deposit interest rates linked to LIBOR.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: If it is clear that someone acted dishonestly to gain a benefit, he should be punished.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked why this new section was required in lieu of strengthening the Securities and Futures Act (SFA).

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The SFA regulates specific financial transactions and products, whereas the fraud offence will cover any kind of dishonest or fraudulent behaviour for gain.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The new fraud offence puts a stop to the game of "catch up" with actors who have a strong financial interest in finding loopholes in regulation.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: So, this law can be used against such actors.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Desmond Choo also asked about how the regime compares with that of foreign jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Desmond Choo also asked about the lack of a materiality requirement in the new offence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Requiring proof of materiality requires a shift of focus back to the victim and how material they found the falsehood, and this is inconsistent with the purpose of the new fraud offence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Christopher de Souza spoke about presumptive minimum sentences.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: But the listed offences do not include provisions in the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA).

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We are not introducing a general doctrine that a mandatory minimum sentence should be replaced by a presumptive minimum sentence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We agree that public education and awareness raising are vital, and we know that the amendments today need to be known beyond this House.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We will continue to work on this together with Members and community partners.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The law can shape social norms, but it is only one factor.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Families, schools, media and the wider community, including non-government organisations, also play important roles in shaping norms, and we look forward to working together.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I believe I have responded to major concerns raised by Members.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza had said, this is a monumental Bill and a law that has been with us for close to 150 years.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The task of this generation is to update it, strengthen it and make it relevant to today’s circumstances.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: This is an opportunity for this House to register our strongest condemnation against acts that harm the most vulnerable among us, persons like Annie Ee, Cindy, Daniel Nasser.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: It is our duty to protect our society against predators like Joshua Robinson and ensure that they get the justice they deserve.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In my speech, I asked the Ministry, there is a provision where the definition of "public servants" where the Police engage law enforcement officers on the ground, such as private security officers or Auxiliary Police Officers, they are treated as public servants if they are carrying out law enforcement, crowd control duties and so on.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: So, would private security officers be treated as public servants in this aspect?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: First, I understand that palliative care and care of that sort would not be constituted as "neglect relating to death".

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But what about refusal to accept medical treatment, or convey the vulnerable adult to medical treatment, when there might be some issue about the adult actually not wanting medical treatment in the first instance?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The second point is on the question I raised about whether there is a possibility, as part of the social norms of sexual offences, that these offences are under-reported in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: This has been the contention that Ms Monica Baey and others have made.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Would the Ministry consider studying this issue to determine whether it is a problem?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: On the issue of palliative arrangement, as I mentioned, it is a fact-sensitive exercise.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The elements of the offence have to be made out, but certain indicators like the evidence of abuse and all that would have to be looked into.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There will be Police investigations, the Courts will have to weigh the evidence, and the Prosecution as well would have to look at the evidence to see whether there is any merit to the complaint.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: So, the intent of the Act, is not to go after bona fide palliative arrangements.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I think that is as far as I could go.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: But quite a lot of it is fact-sensitive.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: On the issue of under-reporting, we are aware this is a global phenomenon.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We have made changes to our various processes, including reporting processes and the provisions today as well.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: These show a clear trajectory that we would like to provide extended support to victims of sexual offences, and we will do what we can.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There will be various studies to see how we can extend our outreach and support people who are in such situations.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: As the amendments are related, may I seek your permission to move them together.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The amendments 1 to 5 proposed in clause 8 are to clarify the objective formulation of “rashness”.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: This is in line with the common law as stated by the High Court in PP vv Hue An Li.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Amendment 6 is to clarify that some offences may have some physical elements which are strict liability and have no corresponding fault elements.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Amendment 7 is to clarify the defence for a strict liability offence, which arises when the accused person shows that he exercised reasonable care in doing all the acts or omissions which are physical elements of the offence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The amendment is to make clear the legislative intent that enhanced penalties for offences committed against domestic workers apply only to employers, members of an employer’s household and employment agents who commit offences against their domestic workers.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The amendment is to make editorial amendments such that for an accused person to rely on a defence of unsoundness of mind, he must not know that what he is doing is wrong by the ordinary standards of reasonable and honest persons, and wrong as contrary to law.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: As the amendments are related, may I seek your permission to move them together?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The amendments are to give effect to the legislative intention that inchoate abetments of offences punishable with death or life imprisonment be punishable with discretionary caning.

speaker: The Chairman
text: For Members who are not following, please refer to the Notice of Amendments to Bill in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: As the amendments are related, may I seek your permission to move them together?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: While this was not proposed by PCRC, the Government reviewed this and is of the view that this should be amended to keep the law updated.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There is value in retaining section 121A, but we should limit its scope.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: In that regard, the Government proposes to remove the words “compasses, imagines, invents, devises or intends”, and replace them with “plans”.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: This will remove the “thought crime” limbs of the offence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The term “plans” refers to early preparatory acts which may fall short of the “substantial step” requirement for attempts or criminal conspiracy to be made out.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: This will allow for authorities to intervene at an earlier stage of planning than what is currently allowed under the law of “attempts” and “criminal conspiracy”.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Whoever plans the death of or hurt to or unlawful imprisonment or restraint of the President, shall be punished with imprisonment for life or for a term which may extend to 20 years and shall, if he is not sentenced to imprisonment for life, also be liable to fine.”.”.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This is the part referred to by Mr Murali Pillai earlier on.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: As the amendments are related, may I seek your permission to move them together?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There is value in retaining section 121B as amended.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The term “plans” refers to early preparatory acts which may fall short of the “substantial step” requirement for attempts or criminal conspiracy to be made out.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: This will allow for authorities to intervene at an earlier stage of planning than what is currently allowed under the law of “attempts” and “criminal conspiracy”.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Whoever plans the unlawful deprivation or deposition of the President from the sovereignty of Singapore, or the overawing by criminal force of the Government, shall be punished with imprisonment for life or for a term which may extend to 20 years and shall, if he is not sentenced to imprisonment for life, also be liable to fine.”.”.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I think this is a very complex Bill and, as a result, there are some of these amendments and we want to be very careful about this.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: So, some of these amendments needed to be made so as not to leave any doubts and cause problems later on.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I apologise for the inconvenience and I think we can get through this quite quickly.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: As the amendments are related, may I seek your permission to move them together?"

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Amendments 1 and 3 clarify the meaning of "premeditation" to make clear that it refers to the fault elements of the accused person arising before the time of the offence.
